items.raw_text: VeriCUA: Verification as Agentic Exploration for Computer-Using Agents Qiushi Sun Affiliation: Google Da Yu Affiliation: Google Alexander Knop Affiliation: Google Amer Sinha Affiliation: Google Lingpeng Kong Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong Ben Kao Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong Ravi Kumar Affiliation: Google Pritish Kamath Corresponding author: qiushisun@connect.hku.hk, pritishk@google.com Affiliation: Google Abstract Building and scaling computer-using agents (CUAs) across desktop, mobile, and web environments requires reliable task-completion verification for data curation, evaluation, and reinforcement learning. Typical automated approaches prompt vision-language models (VLMs) to judge trajectories or generate programs to inspect application state. However, both rely on partial views of complex digital environments. VLM judges are restricted to supplied observations, while generated programs depend on accessible state. These views can omit decisive evidence or leave completion judgments unsupported. Tailoring separate verifiers to different platforms and access settings adds further engineering cost. We present VeriCUA, a platform-agnostic framework for verification through agentic exploration. It treats verification as dynamic evidence gathering and assessment within a shared procedure for online and offline settings across platforms and observation modalities. After inspecting the available context to construct a task rubric, the verifier selects GUI or code checks for unresolved requirements and combines their findings under explicit evidence rules. Experiments show improved agreement with reference labels over the compared baselines across these settings, with the largest offline gains on hard cases and stronger rejection of false completion claims online. Further analyses connect these gains to complementary evidence and test-time exploration. 1 Introduction Vision-language models (VLMs) have enabled computer-using agents (CUAs) to navigate the digital world through software interfaces ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Rawles et al., 2025 ) . Given a natural-language instruction, an agent observes the interface, plans, and acts, leaving a trajectory of thoughts, actions, and observations. Digital tasks span applications in which success can depend on visual presentation, application records, or changes to persisted files. A trajectory can appear successful even when edits remain unsaved or an operation fails without a visible warning. The agent may also report completion after fulfilling only part of the instruction. Accepting such a run as successful produces a false positive, making the distinction between attempted actions and their actual effects central to verification. Developing these agents therefore requires reliable judgments throughout evaluation, data curation ( Sun et al., 2025 ) , and reinforcement learning ( Xue et al., 2026a ) , including applications for which no task-specific checker has been supplied. An execution can be verified online from the resulting machine state or offline from its retained trajectory. Evidence can come from rendered interfaces, structured observations, or artifacts such as files and database records. VLM judges assess trajectories from selected observations ( Pan et al., 2024 ) , while automatically generated checkers inspect application state through model-written programs ( Xue et al., 2026b ) . A fixed set of frames may omit a decisive effect, and a generated query may target state that does not answer the verification question. Platform-native signals support more specialized judgments and validation ( Chae et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026b ) , but their availability varies with the application and access setting. Agentic approaches actively inspect trajectories or environments ( Wan et al., 2026 ; Cui et al., 2026 ; Sanayei et al., 2026 ) . A shared procedure must seek relevant evidence under these access constraints and ground its conclusions in the observations. Figure 1 : VeriCUA inspects the available environment or recording before constructing a rubric, then gathers evidence to verify its requirements. To address these evidence and access limitations, we present VeriCUA, a platform-agnostic framework that formulates CUA verification as agentic exploration (Figure 1 ). It provides a shared procedure for offline and online verification using the sources and inspection tools available in each setting. Verification begins after the executing agent’s attempt ends. The verifier first explores the available context to understand the app and its task artifacts, then uses these observations with the instruction to construct a rubric of fine-grained requirements. This context helps interpret task concepts and locate potential evidence, especially when the application is unfamiliar. The verifier chooses GUI or code tools to check the rubric’s requirements. Findings from these checks reveal what remains unresolved and guide further inspection of relevant frames, artifacts, or another available source. VeriCUA’s unified design separates the verification workflow from the interfaces through which evidence is obtained. Offline verification navigates retained screen frames and action logs, using structured observations such as accessibility trees when recorded. Online verification can inspect the accessible machine state left by the executing agent through GUI or code tools, including files, databases, and system services. These sources answer different questions about the requested outcome. An action log records an attempted edit, while a file read can show whether the edited content persisted. A report that the task is complete remains a claim to verify. The framework links findings to their supporting observations and records source properties such as frame timing or state persistence. Explicit evidence rules combine the findings into a task verdict while retaining which requirements are supported, refuted, or unresolved. We evaluate this shared procedure in offline and online scenarios on multiple platforms. VeriCUA achieves higher agreement with reference labels than the compared baselines in both settings. It also rejects more false completion claims than the VLM judge in the online study. The action-space study shows that adding code-based state reads enables more decisions without increasing false positives. At a matched number of verification passes, adding visual evidence improves agreement and decision coverage compared with repeating the same configuration. Our contributions are summarized below: • General-Purpose Agentic Verification. VeriCUA formulates CUA verification as agentic exploration, providing a shared paradigm for offline and online tasks across platforms and available evidence sources. • Adaptive Evidence Gathering. Context inspection grounds task rubrics in the available environment or recording. The verifier selects GUI or code checks for unresolved requirements and combines findings under source-specific evidence rules. • Evaluation Across Platforms. Experiments show improved agreement with reference labels across the evaluated platforms. Analyses show how evidence access and complementary exploration affect decision coverage and reliability. 2 Related Work Computer-Using Agents and Their Evaluation. These benchmarks typically use task-specific programmatic evaluators to check the resulting application state. Human-labeled trajectory datasets provide reference judgments across applications ( Sun et al., 2026a ) , while audits of benchmark evaluators identify errors in the checks used to produce reference labels ( Xie et al., 2025 ) . Benchmarks of environment-aware judges assess evidence acquisition and verification of states and execution processes ( Shi et al., 2026 ) . Completion judgments also support data curation and training beyond benchmark evaluation. Trajectory synthesis pipelines use verifier scores to select examples ( Sun et al., 2025 ) , and continual reinforcement learning relies on automated feedback during environment adaptation ( Xue et al., 2026a ) . Rubric-based reward modeling further uses synthetic criteria derived from preferred and rejected responses ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Safety-oriented evaluation additionally examines whether agent behavior satisfies workflow constraints ( Sun et al., 2026b ) . items.content: Comparing Human Role-Players and LLM-Simulated Clients in Online Counselling Training: An Analysis of Counselling Patterns Eric Rudolph Philipp Steigerwald Jens Albrecht Address: Technische Hochschule Nürnberg Georg Simon Ohm Address: Nürnberg, Germany Email: {eric.rudolph, philipp.steigerwald, jens.albrecht}@th-nuernberg.de Abstract This study investigates the capabilities of Large Language Models to simulate counselling clients in educational role-plays in comparison to human role-players. Initially, we recorded role-playing sessions, where novice counsellors interacted with human peers acting as clients, followed by role-plays between humans and clients simulated by Mistrals Mixtral 8x7b using 4-bit quantization. These interactions were analysed with a counselling communication pattern system at sentence level. We investigated two key questions: (1) to what extent LLM-generated responses replicate authentic conversational dynamics and (2) whether counsellors’ communication behaviour differs when interacting with human versus LLM-simulated clients. The findings highlight both similarities and differences in the application of counselling patterns across scenarios, showing the potential of LLM-based role-playing exercises to enhance counselling competencies and to identify areas for further refinement in virtual client simulations. keywords Large Language Models, Counselling, Natural Language Processing, Educational Data Mining, AI in Education, Counselling Training, Client Simulation 1 Introduction Text-based online counselling has gained increasing prominence as a flexible and accessible alternative to traditional face-to-face therapy, especially in reaching diverse populations with unique needs [ 5 , 13 ] . Within counsellor education, role-playing exercises are central to developing crucial communication competencies [ 15 , 14 ] , offering trainees controlled, practice-oriented scenarios to explore, reflect on, and refine their skills [ 18 , 20 ] . Help, Problem-Solving: Utterances intended to facilitate problem resolution or offer direct assistance. Generating Motivation: Strategies that evoke or enhance the client’s intrinsic motivation for change. Resource Activation: Identification and mobilization of internal or external resources to support the client. Other Statements: Miscellaneous expressions that do not fit into the main categories. Formalities at the Beginning: Opening formalities such as greetings and introductory remarks. Formalities at the End: Closing formalities including farewells and session summaries. Formalities at the Beginning: Counselor’s introductory remarks and greetings to initiate the session. Formalities at the End: Counselor’s closing remarks and farewells to conclude the session. Analysis & Agreement on Counselling Goals: Counselor’s statements involving the formulation and mutual agreement on counselling goals. The analysis shows an examination of pattern distributions by computing the frequency of each GeCCo category in both Human-Human and Human-LLM interactions. Similarly, Formalities at the End are more common in LLM-generated clients (11.95%) than in human clients (5.95%), probably reflecting structured conversation patterns typical of LLM responses. Help, Problem Solving and Moderation increase as the conversation progresses, especially in Human-Human interactions. This suggests that in the latter stages, human counsellors focus on leading the discussion and addressing the client’s problems. In contrast, these patterns are less pronounced in Human-LLM interactions, suggesting a different conversation dynamic where problem solving does not escalate as much over time. Another noticeable trend is in category Generating Motivation , which remains relatively low throughout the interview but increases slightly towards the end. This could indicate that counsellors are making an effort to introduce motivational interventions before the end of the counselling. Figure 2: Frequency of Predicted Counsellor Labels along Conversation Progression \Description A multi-line chart plotting the normalized frequency of counsellor communication patterns across ten equally-sized segments (deciles) of each session, for Human–Human and Human–LLM interactions. Lines represent patterns such as Analysis/Clarification–Reflection (Factual), Help/Problem-Solving, Moderation, Generating Motivation, Conversation Opening, and Formalities at Beginning/End, illustrating how each pattern rises or falls over the course of the session. In the client interaction patterns (Figure 3 ), Analysis and Clarification of Problems is the predominant category, especially at the beginning of the conversation. This trend is much more pronounced in Human-Human interactions, where problem elaboration starts high (over 8%) and gradually decreases over time. In contrast, LLM-simulated clients disclose their problems more immediately but with less intensity, which is consistent with the results of the overall distribution that showed a lower percentage for this pattern in LLM-generated conversations. A key difference between human and LLM clients is the increase in helping, problem solving, and resource activation in the second half of the conversation, especially in the Human-LLM interactions. This suggests that LLM-generated clients are more inclined to shift to problem-solving and resource-orientated discussions as the conversation progresses, whereas human clients may continue to reflect on their problems. In addition, formality at the beginning is higher of Human-LLM interactions but quickly decreases, while formality at the end increases sharply in the last decile. This reflects the structured nature of LLM-generated responses, which tend to adhere to clear opening and closing conventions. Figure 3: Frequency of Predicted Client Labels along conversation progression \Description A multi-line chart showing the normalized frequency of client communication patterns over ten deciles of session progression for both Human–Human and Human–LLM conversations. Lines denote Analysis Clarification of Problems, Help/Problem-Solving, Resource Activation, Generating Motivation, Formalities at Beginning/End, and Other Statements, highlighting differences in how clients disclose issues and shift toward solutions over time. 5.3 Semantic Analysis To further examine differences in conversational patterns, we applied embedding-based representations using the GBERT-Large Client and Counsellor Classifiers. These models, initially trained for sentence classification, were also used to generate embeddings for client and counsellor messages. The resulting embeddings were visualised using t-SNE to illustrate the clustering of different interaction patterns. The t-SNE projection for client messages (Figure 4) shows that Analysis & Clarification of Problems (orange) is the most dispersed category, indicating that problem elaboration occurs across diverse conversational contexts. In addition to the static t-SNE plot analysis an interactive version has been analysed. It reveals that the orange cluster at the bottom of the client projection corresponds to General Inquiries , which appears more frequently in Human-Human interactions. This suggests that human clients tend to ask general questions more often than LLM clients, possibly because LLM-generated responses are shaped by instruction-following rather than reciprocal questioning. Additionally, Agreement statements appear as a distinct cluster, with LLM-generated agreements tending to be embedded in longer sentences rather than short affirmations. This aligns with our previous findings that human clients engage more extensively in problem clarification, while LLM-simulated clients disclose problems more directly. Another visible cluster in the center of the projection represents negative feedback on prior problem-solving efforts, further suggesting that LLM clients engage in a more structured feedback process compared to human clients. Formalities at the Beginning form a distinct, tightly clustered region, suggesting that these statements play a structurally separate role from the core counselling discussion. Formalities at the End exhibit a similar concentrated pattern, reinforcing the notion that LLM-generated clients tend to follow clear opening and closing conventions, as observed in the pattern distribution. Figure 4: t-SNE Projection of Client Sentences \Description A t-SNE scatter plot of client message embeddings, colored by GeCCo category. The Analysis Clarification of Problems points (orange) are dispersed across the plot, indicating diverse contexts. Tight clusters appear for Formalities at Beginning (top right) and Formalities at End (bottom left). Distinct clusters for Agreement, Help/Problem-Solving, Resource Activation, and Generating Motivation are also visible, demonstrating semantic grouping of client utterances. The t-SNE projection for counsellor messages (Figure 5 ) reveals well-defined clusters for Help, Problem-Solving , reflecting the central role of problem resolution in counselling interactions. Analysis/Clarification - Reflection (Factual) and Analysis/Clarification - Reflection (Emotion) are positioned closely, indicating that factual and emotional reflections frequently co-occur within conversations. A key distinction in Human-LLM interactions emerges in the Analysis/Clarification (Factual) category. An interactive plot analysis reveals that when engaging with human clients, counsellors tend to provide more detailed follow-up questions regarding past solution attempts. Examples include inquiries such as "How did he join your circle of friends?" or "What was it like when you weren’t arguing so often?" This pattern is evident in the lower-right region of the t-SNE

items.content: Science AI We’re inspired by AI’s growing ability to surmount scientific grand challenges. Our team works closely with the research community to pursue breakthrough discoveries and develop new AI tools to accelerate scientific progress. Together, our aim is to supercharge scientific innovation for a better world. Explore more We’re inspired by AI’s growing ability to surmount scientific grand challenges. Our team works closely with the research community to pursue breakthrough discoveries and develop new AI tools to accelerate scientific progress. Together, our aim is to supercharge scientific innovation for a better world. Explore more Collaborative and open science Our history of scientific contributions is rooted in highly collaborative research that promotes transparent, accessible and rigorous results. We develop open source software, release open datasets, and partner with researchers globally. Learn more Tools to accelerate scientific discovery We build AI-powered tools to empower the global scientific community to quickly move from idea to discovery. These experimental tools, including Empirical Research Assistance and AI co-scientist, help scientists tackle complex questions once thought impossible, and solve the world’s most daunting challenges at unprecedented speed. Learn more Decoding biological complexity We use AI to tackle the biggest unsolved questions in biology, from understanding the genome to solving the mysteries of the brain. These insights address core questions that benefit biomedical researchers, and ultimately millions of patients affected by rare genetic and neurological conditions. Using AI to map and understand the brain We are driving progress toward precisely mapping the connections between every cell in the brain. Through an evolving set of AI-based tools for neural reconstruction, analysis, and visualization, we help scientists unlock a deeper understanding of how we think, learn and experience the world. Learn more Using AI to interpret the genome During a decade of applying AI to genomics, we've partnered with labs globally to decode the DNA of humans, animals and plants. Our research enables discoveries and advances healthcare while also providing critical tools to preserve the world’s biodiversity. Learn more Modeling the earth & environment We use AI to improve humanity’s fundamental understanding of Earth’s complex systems: water, land, life and sky. By understanding our planet, we enable communities, researchers and governments to make more informed decisions that foster resilience and achieve a safer, healthier and more sustainable future for all. Flood forecasting Our flood forecasting models use AI to help close the global warning gap, providing reliable flood predictions even in regions that previously lacked data. Learn more Earthquake detection We leverage measurements from a global network of Android smartphones to detect earthquakes and deliver early warnings to people in affected areas. Learn more Wildfire research We use satellite imagery and AI to detect and track the boundaries of wildfires, simulate wildfire evolution, and provide near real-time alerts to help affected communities and responders act fast. Learn more Species mapping As Earth’s biodiversity faces a crisis, we are using AI to map plant, animal and fungi distributions at unprecedented scale. These maps help identify where species live, providing critical data for conservation efforts. Watch the video Atmospheric modeling Our NeuralGCM model combines the best of physics and AI to rapidly, efficiently, and accurately simulate Earth’s atmosphere. This hybrid approach enables researchers to run climate simulations more efficiently than ever before. Learn more Mapping space weather We used aggregated measurements from millions of Android phones to measure the ionosphere and space weather in Earth’s upper atmosphere, doubling global coverage compared to traditional methods. Learn more Featured publications Expert evaluation of LLM world models: A high-Tc superconductivity case study Haoyu Guo Maria Tikhanovskaya Paul Raccuglia Alexey Vlaskin Chris Co Dan Liebling Scott Ellsworth Matthew Abraham Lizzie Dorfman Peter Armitage Chunhan Feng Antoine Georges Olivier Gingras Dominik Kiese Steve Kivelson Vadim Oganesyan Brad Ramshaw Subir Sachdev Senthil Todadri John Tranquada Michael Brenner Subhashini Venugopalan Eun-Ah Kim Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (2026) Preview Preview abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) show great promise as a powerful tool for scientific literature exploration. However, their effectiveness in providing scientifically accurate and comprehensive answers to complex questions within specialized domains remains an active area of research. This work evaluates the performance of six different LLM-based systems for answering scientific literature questions, including commercially available closed models and a custom retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system capable of retrieving images alongside text. We conduct a rigorous expert evaluation of the systems in the domain of high-temperature cuprate superconductors, a research area that involves material science, experimental physics, computation, and theoretical physics. We use an expert-curated database of 1726 scientific papers and a set of 67 expert-formulated questions. The evaluation employs a multi-faceted rubric assessing balanced perspectives, factual comprehensiveness, succinctness, evidentiary support, and image relevance. Our results demonstrate that RAG-based systems, powered by curated data and multimodal retrieval, outperform existing closed models across key metrics, particularly in providing comprehensive and well-supported answers, and in retrieving relevant visual information. This study provides valuable insights into designing and evaluating specialized scientific literature understanding systems, particularly with expert involvement, while also highlighting the importance of rich, domain-specific data in such systems. View details Sexual dimorphism in the complete connectome of the Drosophila male central nervous system Stuart Berg Isabella R Beckett Marta Costa Philipp Schlegel Michał Januszewski Elizabeth C Marin Aljoscha Nern Stephan Preibisch Wei Qiu Shin-ya Takemura Andrew Champion Reed A. George Gary Huang William Katz Christopher Ordish Ken Hayworth Eric Trautman Viren Jain Vivek Jayaraman Wyatt Korff Geoffrey W Meissner Sandro Romani Jan Funke Christopher Knecht Stephan Saalfeld Louis Scheffer Scott Waddell Gwyneth Card Carlos Ribeiro Michael B. Reiser Harald Hess Gerry Rubin Gregory S.X.E. Jefferis Cell (2026) Preview Preview abstract Sex differences in behaviour exist across all animals, typically under strong genetic regulation. In Drosophila, fruitless/doublesex transcription factors can identify dimorphic neurons but their organisation into functional circuits remains unclear. We present the connectome of the entire Drosophila male central nervous system. This contains 166,691 neurons spanning the brain and nerve cord, fully proofread and annotated including fruitless/doublesex expression and 11,691 types. We provide the first comprehensive comparison between male and female brain connectomes to synaptic resolution, finding 7,205 isomorphic, 114 dimorphic, 262 male-specific and 69 female-specific types. This resource enables analysis of full sensory-to-motor circuits underlying complex behaviours and the impact of dimorphic elements. Sex-specific/dimorphic neurons are concentrated in higher brain centres while the sensory and motor periphery are largely isomorphic. Within higher centres, male-specific connections are organised into hotspots defined by male-specific neurons or arbours. Numerous circuit switches reroute sensory information to form antagonistic circuits controlling opposing behaviours. (Full author list included with the paper.) View details An AI system to help scientists write expert-level empirical software Eser Aygün Anastasiya Belyaeva Gheorghe Comanici Marc Coram Hao Cui Jake Garrison Renee Johnston Anton Kast Cory McLean Peter Norgaard Zahra Shamsi David Smalling James Thompson Subhashini Venugopalan Brian Williams Sarah Martinson Martyna Plomecka Lai Wei Yuchen Zhou Qian-Ze Zhu Matthew Abraham Erica Brand Anna Bulanova Jeffrey Cardille Chris Co Scott Ellsworth Grace Joseph Malcolm Kane Ryan Krueger Johan Kartiwa Dan Liebling Jackson Cui Jan-Matthis Lückmann Paul Raccuglia Julie Wang Kat Chou James Manyika Yossi Matias John Platt Lizzie Dorfman Shibl Mourad Michael Brenner Nature (2026) Preview Preview abstract The cycle of scientific discovery is frequently bottlenecked by the slow, manual creation of software to support computational experiments. To address this, we present Empirical Research Assistance (ERA), an AI system that creates expert-level scientific software whose goal is to maximize a quality metric. The system uses a Large Language Model (LLM) and Tree Search (TS) to systematically improve the quality metric and intelligently navigate the large space of possible solutions. ERA achieves expert-level results when it explores and integrates complex research ideas from external sources. The effectiveness of tree search is demonstrated across a diverse range of tasks. Our team works closely with the research community to pursue breakthrough discoveries and develop new AI tools to accelerate scientific progress. Together, our aim is to supercharge scientific innovation for a better world. Explore more We’re inspired by AI’s growing ability to surmount scientific grand challenges. Our team works closely with the research community to pursue breakthrough discoveries and develop new AI tools to accelerate scientific progress. Together, our aim is to supercharge scientific innovation for a better world. Explore more Collaborative and open science Our history of scientific contributions is rooted in highly collaborative research that promotes transparent, accessible and rigorous results. We develop open source software, release open datasets, and partner with researchers globally. Learn more Tools to accelerate scientific discovery We build AI-powered tools to empower the global scientific community to quickly move from idea to discovery. These experimental tools, including Empirical Research Assistance and AI co-scientist, help scientists tackle complex questions once thought impossible, and solve the world’s most daunting challenges at unprecedented speed. Learn more Decoding biological complexity We use AI to tackle the biggest unsolved questions in biology, from understanding the genome to solving the mysteries of the brain. These insights address core questions that benefit biomedical researchers, and ultimately millions of patients affected by rare genetic and neurological conditions. Using AI to map and understand the brain We are driving progress toward precisely mapping the connections between every cell in the brain. Through an evolving set of AI-based tools for neural reconstruction, analysis, and visualization, we help scientists unlock a deeper understanding of how we think, learn and experience the world. Learn more Using AI to interpret the genome During a decade of applying AI to genomics, we've partnered with labs globally to decode the DNA of humans, animals and plants. Our research enables discoveries and advances healthcare while also providing critical tools to preserve the world’s biodiversity. Learn more Modeling the earth & environment We use AI to improve humanity’s fundamental understanding of Earth’s complex systems: water, land, life and sky. By understanding our planet, we enable communities, researchers and governments to make more informed decisions that foster resilience and achieve a safer, healthier and more sustainable future for all. Flood forecasting Our flood forecasting models use AI to help close the global warning gap, providing reliable flood predictions even in regions that previously lacked data. Learn more Earthquake detection We leverage measurements from a global network of Android smartphones to detect earthquakes and deliver early warnings to people in affected areas. Learn more Wildfire research We use satellite imagery and AI to detect and track the boundaries of wildfires, simulate wildfire evolution, and provide near real-time alerts to help affected communities and responders act fast. Learn more Species mapping As Earth’s biodiversity faces a crisis, we are using AI to map plant, animal and fungi distributions at unprecedented scale. These maps help identify where species live, providing critical data for conservation efforts. Watch the video Atmospheric modeling Our NeuralGCM model combines the best of physics and AI to rapidly, efficiently, and accurately simulate Earth’s atmosphere. This hybrid approach enables researchers to run climate simulations more efficiently than ever before. Learn more Mapping space weather We used aggregated measurements from millions of Android phones to measure the ionosphere and space weather in Earth’s upper atmosphere, doubling global coverage compared to traditional methods. However, their effectiveness in providing scientifically accurate and comprehensive answers to complex questions within specialized domains remains an active area of research. This work evaluates the performance of six different LLM-based systems for answering scientific literature questions, including commercially available closed models and a custom retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system capable of retrieving images alongside text. We conduct a rigorous expert evaluation of the systems in the domain of high-temperature cuprate superconductors, a research area that involves material science, experimental physics, computation, and theoretical physics. We use an expert-curated database of 1726 scientific papers and a set of 67 expert-formulated questions. The evaluation employs a multi-faceted rubric assessing balanced perspectives, factual comprehensiveness, succinctness, evidentiary support, and image relevance. Our results demonstrate that RAG-based systems, powered by curated data and multimodal retrieval, outperform existing closed models across key metrics, particularly in providing comprehensive and well-supported answers, and in retrieving relevant visual information. This study provides valuable insights into designing and evaluating specialized scientific literature understanding systems, particularly with expert involvement, while also highlighting the importance of rich, domain-specific data in such systems. We provide the first comprehensive comparison between male and female brain connectomes to synaptic resolution, finding 7,205 isomorphic, 114 dimorphic, 262 male-specific and 69 female-specific types. This resource enables analysis of full sensory-to-motor circuits underlying complex behaviours and the impact of dimorphic elements. Sex-specific/dimorphic neurons are concentrated in higher brain centres while the sensory and motor periphery are largely isomorphic. Within higher centres, male-specific connections are organised into hotspots defined by male-specific neurons or arbours. Numerous circuit switches reroute sensory information to form antagonistic circuits controlling opposing behaviours. (Full author list included with the paper.) items.summary: Make america healthy again President Trump launched the Make America Healthy Again initiative to confront chronic disease, improve nutrition, and lower healthcare costs. This year, the administration advanced reforms targeting childhood health, food quality, and preventive care while increasing transparency and accountability in healthcare systems. These actions are laying the foundation for a healthier, stronger America. items.title: What AI gets wrong and what failure teaches us
items.summary:
Jennifer Neville did not want to go into computer science—but that’s exactly where she landed. Neville discusses the starts and stops that led to her professional sweet spot and her work identifying “surprising failures” making it hard for AI to handle complexity.

The post What AI gets wrong and what failure teaches us appeared first on Microsoft Research.

items.title: Agent Lightning v1.0: A 3,500-Line Lightweight Agentic RL Framework for Training Agents with Real Harnesses

items.content: At a glance Harnessed Agentic RL: Microsoft Research Asia introduces a training paradigm in which the same agent harness used in deployment participates directly in reinforcement learning, removing the need to reimplement the agent inside the training framework. Lightweight by design: Agent Lightning v1.0 delivers a complete agent RL control plane in roughly 3,500 lines of code. Native Kubernetes support: agents run as standard Kubernetes jobs on self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure, with no dependency on paid commercial sandbox services. Data-efficient training recipe: an end-to-end coding agent pipeline raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, a 14.6 percentage point gain, using only about 6,000 training samples based on open sourced dataset. AI agents have evolved from single models to complex full-stack systems built from models, tools, and execution environments. Their capabilities increasingly depend on the agent harness that coordinates them from outside the model. Reinforcement learning (RL) is an approach where AI systems learn through trial and error, guided by rewards and penalties for their actions. RL can make those agents better, but most agent RL systems require developers to reimplement the agent inside the training framework. That is costly, and it means the agent being trained is not quite the agent that gets deployed. To address this, researchers at Microsoft Research Asia have introduced the Harnessed Agentic RL training paradigm and open-sourced a fully rebuilt Agent Lightning v1.0 (opens in new tab) . Compared with the original, Agent Lightning, v1.0 puts more emphasis on staying lightweight, on integrating with real harnesses, and on a complete, reproducible agent RL training pipeline. Agent Lightning v1.0 was rebuilt around Harnessed Agentic RL, with key improvements: Lightweight : the entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code. Agent Lightning v1.0 implements a complete Harnessed Agentic RL system in a codebase that is small and clear enough to understand, modify, and extend. Training on a real agent harness : agents reach the model through the large language model (LLM) proxy in Agent Lightning v1.0, leaving existing harness code unchanged. Native Kubernetes support : agents run directly as Kubernetes jobs, without external commercial sandbox services. Self-managed clusters and local infrastructure alike can support rollouts at scale. A complete coding agent training example : an end-to-end pipeline built on Qwen3.5-9B raised Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified from 41.8% to 56.4%, an absolute gain of 14.6 percentage points, using only about 6,000 training samples. The limits of traditional agentic RL Traditional agentic RL assumes the training framework owns the interaction loop with the environment. In a ReAct-style loop, the model generates an action, the environment returns an observation, the observation is appended to the context, and the model generates the next action, so the whole rollout maps onto one continuous token trajectory. Early RL systems such as verl, AReaL, and slime were built this way, which meant training an agent required rebuilding its loop inside the RL framework. Real harnesses have outgrown that assumption. Coding agents such as mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex each bring their own context management, tool protocols, execution logic, and dependencies, as do general-purpose agent systems. Rebuilding one for training is expensive, and the rebuilt agent may no longer behave in the same way as the deployed agent. Agent Lightning takes a different route. It places an LLM proxy between the agent and the model. The agent continues to run as before: simply point the endpoint that previously called the model API at Agent Lightning, and the training framework can observe and record its model calls. In v1.0, the researchers go further and formally define this paradigm as Harnessed Agentic RL: whichever agent harness is used in deployment is the harness that takes part directly in reinforcement learning during training (Figure 1). Figure 1. Traditional agentic RL compared with Harnessed Agentic RL. In traditional agentic RL, the training framework manages the environment and the agent loop. In Harnessed Agentic RL, the harness manages both. Four challenges in training with real harnesses A core difference between Harnessed Agentic RL and traditional agentic RL is that the environment interaction loop is handled by the agent harness rather than the training framework. The training system can only observe a series of LLM request and response pairs, so a single rollout may be split into a variable number of training samples. This brings four key challenges: Retokenization and sample merging : Harnesses keep context as text, but RL training needs the token IDs sampled during the rollout. Passing text through the chat template and tokenizer again can shift token boundaries, so adjacent calls cannot always be merged into one sample. Advantage calculation : Retokenization, subagents and context summarization can split one rollout into several samples. Computing baselines and advantages directly at the sample level causes rollouts that produce more samples to be counted repeatedly, which alters the original statistical relationships at the rollout level. Loss normalization : Averaging loss by sample count gives more weight to rollouts that produce more samples. Since sample count is often just a product of harness behavior, loss normalization must also avoid being distorted by it. Training backend scheduling : Sample count and length are known only after the harness finishes, while GPU counts and data/tensor parallel configurations are usually fixed. The backend has to map a variable workload into fixed resources. Microsoft Research StorY OptiMind: When the system meets the floor A three‑month pilot in a Midwestern bottling plant shows what happens when AI moves beyond chat and into decision-making, where constraints shift, stakes are real, and answers must hold. Learn more Opens in a new tab Building a complete agent RL control plane in 3,500 lines of code In system design, Agent Lightning v1.0 treats simplicity as its first principle. The entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code, with three core components: the API Gateway, the Rollout Controller, and the Customized Trainer (Figure 2). The API gateway stores rollouts, models, and events, and serves as an OpenAI-compatible LLM proxy. It links every model call from the harness to its rollout and records the prompts, responses, and log probabilities that training needs. The rollout controller starts and manages agent execution, either as local processes or as standard Kubernetes jobs, keeping agent execution separate from the trainer. The customized trainer, built on verl, creates rollouts, waits for them to finish, collects samples, and assembles the final training samples through a sample adapter. As a result, for an existing agent harness, simply pointing the model endpoint at the Agent Lightning proxy is usually enough to connect quickly to RL training. Figure 2. The Agent Lightning v1.0 system architecture showing the API gateway, rollout controller, and customized trainer. Collocated async RL Rollout times vary widely across agents. Synchronous RL waits for the slowest agent in a batch and leaves GPUs idle, while fully asynchronous RL raises utilization but needs separate GPU pools for rollout and training. In response, Agent Lightning v1.0 introduces Collocated Async RL, which lets rollout and model updates share the same set of GPUs. Once the system has collected enough rollouts, the update begins: the API Gateway pauses accepting new requests and waits for requests already in progress to finish, and rollout resumes after the update completes. The entire state transition is transparent to the external agent harness. In experiments, this approach achieved about a 2x end-to-end speedup over synchronous RL while using fewer GPUs than conventional asynchronous RL (Figure 3). Figure 3. Synchronous RL, asynchronous RL, and Collocated Async RL compared. Collocated Async RL raises utilization while occupying fewer GPUs. Running agents on Kubernetes Collecting enough rollouts means running many agents at once, which consumes substantial CPU, memory, and compute resources. Other Harnessed Agentic RL frameworks often host those agents on commercial sandbox services such as Modal Sandbox or E2B, where cost climbs quickly with scale. Instead, Agent Lightning v1.0 runs them as standard Kubernetes jobs, reusing existing self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure (Figure 4). Existing compute resources are used more efficiently, large rollouts cost less, and the whole pipeline stays open source and reproducible. Figure 4. The Rollout Controller in Agent Lightning v1.0 provides native Kubernetes support, running agents directly as standard Kubernetes jobs. 6,000 training samples, a 14.6-point performance gain To test the approach, researchers built a full pipeline on SWE-smith, mini-SWE-agent, and Qwen3.5-9B, covering data cleaning, environment construction, reward-hacking safeguards, and RL training. The training set holds about 6,000 samples and needs no large-scale compute. RL training alone raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% on SWE-bench Verified, a gain of 14.6 percentage points. The coding agent experiments further confirm the earlier analysis of two challenges: advantage calculation and loss normalization. Compared with sample-level handling, rollout-level advantage combined with rollout-level normalization achieves a higher validation reward and keeps policy entropy more stable during training (Figure 5). Figure 5. Pass rate and policy entropy for Qwen3.5-9B on the SWE-smith validation set. items.title: Proof-based general-purpose computing with Magnetar
items.summary: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. items.content: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program. Three grand challenges Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time. Efficiency . Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere. Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security. Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029 . Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions. Spotlight: Event Series Microsoft Research Forum Join us for a continuous exchange of ideas about research in the era of general AI. Watch the latest episodes on demand. Watch on-demand Opens in a new tab More than a decade of work For more than a decade, Microsoft Research has worked on making zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing practical. Early research followed two approaches, both practical only for small programs. The first (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) lets a verifier check a long computation through a short conversation with the prover using a technique called the sum-check protocol (opens in new tab) , but this applied only to computations with a particular layered structure. The second (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) used elliptic-curve cryptography to create very small proofs for almost any computation. But this requires a one-time trusted setup involving secret information which, if leaked, could allow anyone to forge proofs. This approach is also vulnerable to quantum computers. In 2019, a new zero-knowledge proof system called Spartan returned to the sum-check approach and made it work for general-purpose programs without a trusted setup. Spartan can also be instantiated with different cryptographic building blocks. That flexibility is what later allowed the proof system to be built on hash functions alone. A sequence of results then filled in the remaining pieces: Phalanx (opens in new tab) , in 2021, showed how to exploit repetition, such as a processor running the same instruction cycle on every step, to prove computations an order of magnitude faster than Spartan. Magnetar’s processor description is built on this idea. Nova (opens in new tab) , HyperNova (opens in new tab) , NeutronNova (opens in new tab) , Neo and SuperNeo (opens in new tab) showed that stopping Spartan’s proving early, and folding the partial results together, makes it practical to prove computations of any size at far lower cost. Brakedown (opens in new tab) , in 2021, introduced a fast hash-based commitment scheme and combined it with Spartan, giving the first Spartan variant whose security rests on standard hash functions. Spice (opens in new tab) , Lasso (opens in new tab) , Nebula (opens in new tab) , and then Twist and Shout (opens in new tab) made the memory operations at the heart of a general-purpose processor inexpensive to prove, and Jolt (opens in new tab) showed that combining them with Spartan can efficiently prove the execution of a complete processor. Earlier this year, Vega (opens in new tab) applied this line of work to digital identity, proving facts from a government credential in under a tenth of a second . More recently, BinarySpartan (opens in new tab) brought Spartan to binary fields, where a processor’s logic and standard hash functions can be efficiently expressed. BinarySpartan also relies on Ligerito (opens in new tab) , a Brakedown-style commitment scheme with much shorter proofs, and on ring switching (opens in new tab) , which makes it efficient to commit to vectors of bits. Each of these solved a piece of the problem. Magnetar is where the pieces come together. Magnetar Magnetar is a zero-knowledge virtual machine, or zkVM, and it makes major progress on all three challenges at once. Figure 1. Magnetar proves a program’s execution and returns a small proof that anyone can check, with security resting only on standard hash functions. It is general-purpose. Magnetar proves the execution of RISC-V, an open processor architecture with mature compilers for every mainstream language. A developer writes a program in Rust, Go, or C, compiles it as usual, and Magnetar proves it as written. Consider what this means in practice. A business policy, a data pipeline, or an interpreter for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is just a program, and the engineers who already maintain it can prove their executions exactly as written. As a result, proving stops being a specialist activity. It is faster than prior systems in the same class. Magnetar proves 7.2 to 8.7 million processor instructions per second on a laptop. Across 15 benchmark programs, from cryptographic hashing to token transfers inside a small EVM interpreter, it is 10 to 39 times faster on average than the fastest existing zkVMs on the same machine, and more than 300 times faster than two others on a token-transfer benchmark. An optimized Magnetar proves 9.5–12.8 million cycles per second, which increases each speedup reported here by about 1.3×. Its proofs verify in about 12 milliseconds. Its security rests on standard cryptography. Magnetar depends on a standard hash function such as SHA-256 or SHA-3, the same primitives that already protect every organization’s systems. It requires no elliptic curves, no lattices, no special-purpose hash functions, no trusted setup, and no unproven conjecture about error-correcting codes. Hash functions are the most thoroughly studied primitives in the cryptographic toolkit, and they are the basis of the stateless hash-based signatures that NIST standardized as its own conservative post-quantum option. For a system that must still be trustworthy in many decades to come, relying only on standard hash functions removes a cryptographic migration from the roadmap. The same design decision pays a second dividend. Checking a Magnetar proof consists mostly of evaluating standard hash functions and binary-field arithmetic, which are exactly the operations Magnetar proves efficiently. Verifying a proof is therefore an ordinary workload for it. This is what allows Magnetar to prove computations of any size, by proving them in pieces and then combining the pieces. This also allows Magnetar to prove a long-running system such as a ledger or a blockchain. The technical paper gives the full design, security analysis, and measurements. Looking ahead Magnetar advances zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing to a stage where they can be built on the cryptography that organizations already trust, at speeds that make it usable, by engineers who write normal code. Magnetar enables a future where cryptographic proofs are a routine output of computation. We expect that technology leaders will stop asking whether proofs of execution are practical and focus instead on which results would they prefer to verify rather than taking on trust . If you’re interested in exploring how zero-knowledge proofs can support your use case, we’d love to hear from you (opens in new tab) . items.content: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. ACADEMIC CONFERENCE Microsoft at SOSP 2026 Academic and industrial participants present research and experience papers that cover the full range of theory and practice of computer systems software. Learn more Opens in a new tab The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project. Opens in a new tab Related publications An O(1) Bound for the KLS Constant Meet the authors Xinzhi Zhang Senior Researcher Learn more Research Areas Artificial intelligence Mathematics

In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project. Catch up on the ideas, tools, and discoveries researchers are exploring today and get a quick look at what’s coming next. Related links: Research Focus newsletter on LinkedIn (opens in new tab) ForkPilot: Self-Evolving Policy for Retrospective Search in Long-Horizon Agents Code Understanding is a Bottleneck for Coding Agents TeleTune: Evolving Agent Skills from Offline Telemetry Why Copilot use looks so similar across industries, and what that misses (opens in new tab) Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools New AI framework bridges a critical gap in mid-range weather forecasts BioEmu2 in public preview (opens in new tab) Chapters 00:48: A self-improving agentic framework (opens in new tab) 01:35: Understanding coding agent success and failure (opens in new tab) 02:29: Evolving agent skills with activity logs (opens in new tab) 03:22: Looking beyond similarities in AI use (opens in new tab) 04:15: Helping teachers make more time for teaching (opens in new tab) 04:52: Improving extended-range weather forecasting (opens in new tab) 05:42: BioEmu2 now available in public preview (opens in new tab) 06:32: Final thoughts (opens in new tab) Subscribe to the Microsoft Research Podcast : Apple Podcasts Email Android Spotify RSS Feed Transcript [MUSIC] SOWBHAGYA SURESH: Hi, I’m Sowbhagya Suresh. Welcome to Microsoft Research Focus . You’ve probably read our newsletter. And now you can get highlights from across the research community at Microsoft here, on YouTube, and major podcast platforms. Whether you read, watch, or listen to it, Research Focus is your source for research news at Microsoft. Coming up in this edition: what everyday AI use reveals about the way we work; how a new AI model could help scientists better understand proteins; a new approach to improving weather forecasts weeks in advance; and more. So here’s what’s new. A self-improving agentic framework More and more, AI agents are handling tasks that are complex. [MUSIC FADES] Tasks that require multiple steps, decisions, and interactions with external tools. But how can we count on AI agents to do the work if their ability to adjust when things go wrong may require a lot of resources with no guarantees of a better result? A new self-improving framework called ForkPilot learns when it’s worth revisiting earlier decisions to find a different approach and adapts its strategy based on new outcomes. Tested across six benchmarks and leading AI models, ForkPilot measures up to the best existing methods while reducing AI processing demands by up to 59%. These results suggest that AI agents can solve complex problems more reliably and efficiently, making them more practical and cost-effective to deploy at scale. [TRANSITION MUSIC] Understanding coding agent success and failure Coding agents execute user queries by reasoning about, editing, and running code. Understanding why these agents fail is critical if we want to build more capable and reliable coding agents. Unfortunately, existing benchmarks often make it difficult to identify which factors contribute to success or failure. CABRA is a framework for generating coding challenges from scratch. It lets researchers increase complexity in a controlled way and pinpoints the skills that are most difficult for agents. Across thousands of generated challenges, the researchers found that agents often overcame coding problems by using tools. Yet the agents still struggled when they needed to understand unfamiliar codebases. The findings suggest that understanding existing code, rather than modifying it, remains one of the biggest obstacles to developing more effective coding agents. [TRANSITION MUSIC] Evolving agent skills with activity logs Computer-use agents are AI systems that are designed to complete tasks that require clicking and typing. They can fill in forms, process requests, and navigate websites. To do this effectively, they need to learn the procedures that people use to get work done. User activity logs can offer a way to capture this knowledge. But activity logs typically don’t record the intent behind each action and often combine tasks. The new framework TeleTune learns reusable skills and workflows from these logs. It also infers the task goals associated with the sequences of actions. In evaluations across software and browser tasks, TeleTune outperformed existing approaches. By learning from existing activity, TeleTune offers a scalable way to help AI agents adapt to unfamiliar software and carry out complex, multi-step workflows [TRANSITION MUSIC] Looking beyond similarities in AI use (opens in new tab) Workers across industries may appear to be using AI in surprisingly similar ways, but a closer look reveals a different story. Microsoft researchers analyzed aggregated Copilot Chat activity across a broad range of customer categories and found that editing documents led all classified activities, accounting for more than 20 percent. But when researchers set aside the 20 most common activities, differences between customer categories became substantially more pronounced. The most common uses of AI may be hiding important differences in how organizations use it for more specialized work. For business leaders, the takeaway is clear: don’t assume you have the same AI needs as others in your industry. Finding the right opportunities means looking beyond usage statistics to understand what employees actually do, how they work, and what outcomes matter most. [TRANSITION MUSIC] Helping teachers make more time for teaching A new study shows how Shiksha Copilot—a human-in-the-loop AI tool—could transform teacher workflows in Global South classrooms. The study in low-resource schools in India found the tool reduced the time teachers spent on bilingual lesson planning and bureaucracy. That gave them more time to craft more engaging classroom activities. More than a thousand teachers participated, and many reported reduced stress levels and a positive impression of how AI can help them. These teachers actively engaged with Shiksha Copilot, using their professional expertise to adapt and repurpose materials to suit their own classrooms. [TRANSITION MUSIC] Improving extended-range weather forecasting Ten-day weather forecasts have become remarkably dependable. But what about the weeks that follow? The two-to-six-week window remains a major challenge for forecasting models, which is a problem. That’s when a wide range of critical decisions get made related to farming, managing wildfires, and preparing for extreme weather. A new machine-learning framework called Probabilistic Bias Correction, or PBC , is helping close that gap. PBC learns from a weather model’s past mistakes and helps correct them. And the early results are promising. PBC took top honors in a global competition focused on improving extended-range forecasting. It’s also being deployed in Kenya, where it’s helping improve critical monsoon forecasts for farmers. This development could help make weather predictions more useful across a broad range of applications. [TRANSITION MUSIC] BioEmu2 now available in public preview (opens in new tab) BioEmu2, a new foundation model for understanding biomolecular structure, dynamics, and function, is now available in public preview. Developed by the Microsoft Research AI for Science team, BioEmu2 builds on Biomolecular Emulator, a deep-learning model designed to help scientists better understand how proteins work. That understanding could have important implications for medicine. By learning more about how proteins function, scientists could move closer to developing more effective medications that enhance beneficial protein activity or prevent proteins from causing harm. Go to the BioEmu2 Microsoft Research GitHub repository (opens in new tab) to explore the model and learn more. [MUSIC] And that’s your Research Focus . From more capable AI agents to better weather forecasting, these are just a few of the developments researchers are exploring at Microsoft. Want to learn more and stay connected? Explore the latest research, discover the people behind it, and keep tabs on the ideas shaping what’s next by following Microsoft Research on major social platforms. I’m Sowbhagya Suresh. Thanks so much for tuning in. We’ll see you in the next Microsoft Research Focus.
