items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.40654 (cs) [Submitted on 29 Oct 2026] Title: Propose-Filter-Release: Scaling Noise to Typical Sensitivity via Private Filtering Authors: Moshe Shenfeld , Eliad Tsfadia , Katrina Ligett View a PDF of the paper titled Propose-Filter-Release: Scaling Noise to Typical Sensitivity via Private Filtering, by Moshe Shenfeld and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: An estimator can be accurate and stable on typical data, yet sensitive to a few possible records. Differentially private mechanisms commonly scale their noise to the worst-case influence of a single record, which lets these records dictate the noise even when the remaining data would allow far less. Removing them first would restore the smaller scale, but the removal must itself be private. We introduce \emph{propose-filter-release} (PFR), which, by privately filtering its input, turns a mechanism that protects the addition or removal of a typical record, one that fits the remaining data, into one that is differentially private in the standard sense, on every input. Using our novel filtering step, PFR requires only a concave friendliness score, which measures how well a record fits a dataset, and a release mechanism that is friendly-DP, that is, private when the changed record fits the remaining data. For every such score and release mechanism, it guarantees differential privacy under public conditions on the number of records, so it is a general privacy primitive, comparable to propose-test-release, and FriendlyCore can be viewed as one of its implementations. We illustrate the generality of PFR by instantiating it for scalar statistics, principal subspace estimation, the KL divergence of user histograms, the effective resistances of a graph, and treatment-rule selection. items.content: Propose-Filter-Release: Scaling Noise to Typical Sensitivity via Private Filtering Moshe Shenfeld † † thanks: Equal contribution. † † thanks: School of Computer Science and Engineering, The Hebrew University of Jerusalem. E-mail: moshenfeld@gmail.com . Eliad Tsfadia 1 1 footnotemark: 1 † † thanks: Department of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, Bar-Ilan University. E-mail: eliad.tsfadia@biu.ac.il . Katrina Ligett † † thanks: School of Computer Science and Engineering, The Hebrew University of Jerusalem. E-mail: katrina.ligett@mail.huji.ac.il . Abstract An estimator can be accurate and stable on typical data, yet sensitive to a few possible records. Differentially private mechanisms commonly scale their noise to the worst-case influence of a single record, which lets these records dictate the noise even when the remaining data would allow far less. Removing them first would restore the smaller scale, but the removal must itself be private. We introduce propose-filter-release (PFR), which, by privately filtering its input, turns a mechanism that protects the addition or removal of a typical record, one that fits the remaining data, into one that is differentially private in the standard sense, on every input. Using our novel filtering step, PFR requires only a concave friendliness score, which measures how well a record fits a dataset, and a release mechanism that is friendly-DP, that is, private when the changed record fits the remaining data. For every such score and release mechanism, it guarantees differential privacy under public conditions on the number of records, so it is a general privacy primitive, comparable to propose-test-release, and FriendlyCore can be viewed as one of its implementations. We illustrate the generality of PFR by instantiating it for scalar statistics, principal subspace estimation, the KL divergence of user histograms, the effective resistances of a graph, and treatment-rule selection. 1 Introduction Statistical analysis estimates patterns shared by a population from data contributed by individuals. When these data are sensitive, the results should not reveal much about any single contributor. Differential privacy (DP) [ 21 ] makes this requirement precise: a randomized algorithm is differentially private if changing the data of any single individual barely changes the distribution of its output. This must hold for every pair of datasets that differ in one individual, including datasets on which the analysis is not expected to be accurate. For convenience, we model a change of one individual’s data as replacing their record with a null placeholder, which is essentially the same as removing it, and equivalent, up to constant factors in the privacy parameters, to replacing it with another record ( Section 2 ). The goals of statistics and of privacy pull in different directions. In particular, privacy must also protect a record whose change would move the result substantially. A statistical analysis, by contrast, is concerned with typical data, in which the records follow a common pattern and no single record has much influence on the result. Noise that protects the worst case is calibrated to records that typical data do not contain, so on typical data it can be disproportionate to the influence of any of their records. The goal of this paper is a general technique whose noise reflects the influence of records on typical data, while it remains private on every dataset. On atypical datasets, it may fail or return an uninformative answer. An illustrative example. We illustrate this goal with principal subspace estimation. Given independent samples from a centered Gaussian distribution in ℝ d {\mathbb{R}}^{d} , the task is to estimate the subspace spanned by the k k leading eigenvectors of its covariance, which are the directions along which the data vary the most. An estimate is accurate when every unit vector in it lies close to this subspace. On such data the samples concentrate near the target subspace, as the samples of Figure 2 do in the plane, and for the covariances that we consider, a non-private estimate is accurate from a number of samples that grows with k k but not with the ambient dimension d d ( Section 5.2 ). A straightforward private approach adds noise that does not depend on the data at hand, and the number of samples that it needs grows polynomially with d d ( Section 5.2 ). In this example, the goal above is a private algorithm that needs, for the data that we consider, a number of samples without a polynomial dependence on d d , as in the non-private case. Global and local sensitivity. The most common way to achieve DP adds noise calibrated to the global sensitivity of the target statistic, the largest change in it between any two neighboring datasets [ 21 ] . This worst-case calibration is private on every dataset, but it ignores the structure that makes typical data easy, and it is the source of the disproportionate noise described above. One hope is to replace the worst-case bound by an instance-dependent one: the local sensitivity of a statistic at a dataset is its largest change between this dataset and one of its neighbors [ 44 ] , and it can be much smaller on typical data. A second hope is to rely on a bound on the local sensitivity only after privately testing that the data satisfy it. The idea is to treat the bad inputs and the typical ones separately, with guarantees governed by the structure of the typical input at hand, as in the beyond-worst-case analysis of algorithms [ 48 ] and in instance-dependent private estimation [ 44 , 5 ] . Under the retention conditions of an application, it removes nothing from typical inputs with high probability, and its accuracy then follows their typical sensitivity. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.40649 (cs) [Submitted on 29 Oct 2026] Title: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations Authors: Nicolas Dufour , Elouan Gardès , Amil Dravid , Patrick Pérez , Loic Landrieu View a PDF of the paper titled Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations, by Nicolas Dufour and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: The Neural Thickets hypothesis posits that pretrained language models lie in dense neighborhoods of task-specific experts in weight space, which random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. We reproduce the reported gains, but show that they do not require this geometric explanation. Perturbing a single decoder block already recovers much of the improvement, while keeping the model entirely frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks. This suggests an alternative explanation based on output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting. We formalize this view as Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), a general procedure that generates perturbed predictors, selects high-performing members on a small validation set, and aggregates their predictions. This interpretation connects Neural Thickets to established inference-time methods, including sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection. A first-order analysis further shows that small weight perturbations act primarily through their induced logit shifts. We extend this analysis to vision, where logit PSV substantially improves performance under domain shift, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations provide little additional benefit. Together, these results suggest that the gains attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead be obtained through output diversity, selection, and voting. Logit PSV realizes these benefits with a fully frozen model, providing a simple, training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision. items.content: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations Nicolas Dufour Affiliation: Kyutai Email: nicolas.dufour@kyutai.org Elouan Gardès Affiliation: Meta FAIR Affiliation: LIGM, CNRS, Univ Gustave Eiffel, ENPC, IP Paris Amil Dravid Affiliation: UC Berkeley Patrick Pérez † † thanks: Work done while at Kyutai. Affiliation: Google DeepMind Loic Landrieu Affiliation: LIGM, CNRS, Univ Gustave Eiffel, ENPC, IP Paris Abstract The Neural Thickets hypothesis posits that pretrained language models lie in dense neighborhoods of task-specific experts in weight space, which random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. We reproduce the reported gains, but show that they do not require this geometric explanation. Perturbing a single decoder block already recovers much of the improvement, while keeping the model entirely frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks. This suggests an alternative explanation based on output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting. We formalize this view as Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), a general procedure that generates perturbed predictors, selects high-performing members on a small validation set, and aggregates their predictions. This interpretation connects Neural Thickets to established inference-time methods, including sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection. A first-order analysis further shows that small weight perturbations act primarily through their induced logit shifts. We extend this analysis to vision, where logit PSV substantially improves performance under domain shift, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations provide little additional benefit. Together, these results suggest that the gains attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead be obtained through output diversity, selection, and voting. Logit PSV realizes these benefits with a fully frozen model, providing a simple, training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision. Project page can be found here: https://kyutai.org/logit-psv . 1 Introduction Gan & Isola (2026) reported a striking phenomenon: randomly perturbing the weights of a pretrained language model can produce many variants that outperform it on specific reasoning tasks. The empirical gains are substantial, reaching up to 52.8 52.8 accuracy points (Countdown with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, from 10.8 % 10.8\% to 63.6 % 63.6\% ), and require little compute compared to fine-tuning. The authors propose a geometric explanation: pretrained weights of sufficiently large models are surrounded by a dense thicket of task-specialized models, recoverable by blind Gaussian perturbations. This paper first asks whether the gain requires perturbing the entire network. It does not: perturbing only a small fraction of the model, or even a single decoder block, recovers much of the gain. Pushing this observation to its limit, weight perturbations can be removed altogether: the model is kept completely frozen and only its output is perturbed: each member differs by a random Gaussian bias, fixed throughout autoregressive generation, added to the logits before greedy decoding. This logit-only variant performs no additional computation inside the network and modifies no model weight. Nevertheless, it recovers, and in some settings improves on, the gains of full-weight perturbations. On OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, it raises MATH-500 accuracy from 63.3 % 63.3\% to 81.3 % 81.3\% , compared with 74.7 % 74.7\% for the full-weight perturbation ensemble. Full-weight PSV (neural thickets) Logit PSV (ours) f 𝜽 f_{{\bm{\theta}}} + + σ ​ ϵ i ∈ ℝ d 𝜽 \sigma\bm{\epsilon}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{{\bm{\theta}}}} into weights f 𝜽 + σ ​ ϵ i f_{{\bm{\theta}}+\sigma\bm{\epsilon}_{i}} logits ℓ i \bm{\ell}_{i} × N \times N perturbed copies of all d 𝜽 ∼ 10 9 d_{{\bm{\theta}}}\!\sim\!10^{9} weights f 𝜽 f_{{\bm{\theta}}} (frozen) ℓ \bm{\ell} + + σ ​ ϵ i ∈ ℝ V \sigma\bm{\epsilon}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{V} into logits ℓ + σ ​ ϵ i \bm{\ell}+\sigma\bm{\epsilon}_{i} one frozen network, × N \times N logit biases, size V ∼ 10 5 V\!\sim\!10^{5} Select Retain top K K on validation set 0.82 0.82 0.51 0.51 0.78 0.78 Logits Validation accuracy Vote Aggregate on test vote prediction Figure 1: Full-weight PSV versus logit PSV. Both methods share the same selection and voting stages ( right ), but differ in the perturbation ( left ). Neural Thickets ( top ) perturb the full d 𝜽 d_{{\bm{\theta}}} -dimensional parameter vector, producing N N distinct networks. Logit PSV ( bottom ) keeps one frozen network and adds a V V -dimensional bias to the output logits, fixed across decoding steps and inputs. The Neural Thickets interpretation attributes these gains to local experts in weight space. Our experiments suggest a simpler account: perturbations induce output diversity, validation-based selection retains useful members, and voting aggregates their predictions. Neural Thickets can therefore be viewed as an instance of a broader perturb-select-vote (PSV) template: sample random perturbations, score the resulting members on a small validation set, retain the top K K , and vote at test time. This output-space view connects PSV to standard inference-time methods. A logit bias modifies the relative probability of each token, and greedy decoding under random biases defines a perturb-and-MAP sampler ( Papandreou & Yuille, 2011 ) . Selecting members by validation performance retains the biases that perform best on the target task, analogously to best-of- N N and verifier-guided selection ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , while voting relates PSV to self-consistency ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . A first-order analysis further supports this view: small weight perturbations act, to leading order, through the logit shifts they induce. This paper then isolates the roles of sampling, selection, and voting: on strong base models, temperature-tuned sampling with majority voting already matches full-weight PSV, showing that output diversity and ensembling explain most of the gain. On weaker models, validation-based selection remains important as it filters unreliable members before aggregation. Finally, the analysis extends to pretrained vision models under domain shift. In this setting, the analogue of a task expert is a domain expert: a perturbed representation that improves linear-probe performance on a target domain. Full-weight PSV, which perturbs the vision backbone and fits one probe per member, is compared to logit-only PSV, which fits a single probe and perturbs only the resulting class logits. The results support the same conclusion as in language: perturbing the logits is sufficient to recover the gains of full-weight perturbations, and often improves out-of-domain performance while leaving the backbone unchanged. Our results do not rule out useful structure in the neighborhood of pretrained weights. They show, however, that such structure is not required to obtain the observed gains. PSV is better understood as output diversification, validation-based filtering, and ensembling. Beyond its role in interpreting Neural Thickets, PSV yields a simple, training-free output-space procedure that substantially improves performance on specialized tasks and domains. Contributions. • Full-weight perturbations are unnecessary. Perturbing even a single decoder block recovers much of the gain of full-weight perturbations. • Logit PSV. Applying PSV directly to the output logits of a fully frozen model matches full-weight perturbation ensembles on reasoning tasks, and sometimes exceeds them. • An output-space interpretation of PSV. Perturbations induce output diversity, selection retains high-reward members, voting aggregates their predictions, and a first-order analysis connects weight perturbations to their induced logit shifts. • Extension to vision. Under domain shift, output-space perturbations recover the gains of full-weight perturbations for pretrained vision backbones as well. 2 Related Work Test-time sampling, selection, and voting. Inference-time scaling improves fixed models by generating multiple candidates and aggregating or selecting them. Self-consistency votes over sampled reasoning paths ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , while best-of- N N selects candidates using a verifier or reward model ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) ; more generally, increasing inference-time compute can substantially improve performance ( Snell et al., 2025 ) . Perturb-and-MAP provides a classical connection between perturbation and sampling, where random logit perturbations followed by MAP inference induce samples from a target distribution ( Papandreou & Yuille, 2011 ; Maddison et al., 2017 ) . Neural Thickets ( Gan & Isola, 2026 ) combines these ingredients: perturbations of the weights generate candidate models, validation performance selects them, and voting aggregates their predictions. Logit-space control. Many methods alter the behavior of a frozen model directly through its logits, including classifier-free guidance ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) , contrastive decoding ( Li et al., 2023 ) , post-hoc calibration ( Guo et al., 2017 ) , and watermarking, which biases a pseudo-random subset of token logits to embed a detectable signal ( Kirchenbauer et al., 2023 ) . These methods design or fit a particular logit transformation for a desired behavior. In contrast, logit PSV uses task-agnostic random biases and relies on selection and voting to exploit the resulting output diversity. Perturbations in weight space. Previous work has revealed substantial structure in the local geometry of neural-network parameters, including mode connectivity ( Garipov et al., 2018 ) , model averaging ( Izmailov et al., 2018 ; Wortsman et al., 2022 ) , and low-dimensional adaptation ( Li et al., 2018 ; Hu et al., 2022 ) . Random weight perturbations are also central to evolution strategies and zeroth-order optimization ( Salimans et al., 2017 ) . Our focus is different: rather than optimizing or merging perturbations, we ask which aspects of weight-space perturbation are actually necessary for the gains of PSV. Additional related work is discussed in Appendix A . 3 The Perturb-Select-Vote Framework 0 0 5 5 10 10 15 15 20 20 25 25 30 30 70 70 80 80 90 90 full weight perturbation no perturbation index of perturbed decoder block countdown acc.(%) single block perturbation Figure 2: Effect of perturbing individual decoder blocks. The central interpretation of Gan & Isola (2026) is that these gains reveal local task experts near the pretrained weights. This interpretation rests on three main claims. First, a density claim: as model size increases, a larger fraction of nearby perturbations improves task performance. Second, a specialist claim: perturbations that improve one task tend to hurt others, suggesting task-specific specialization. Together, these claims frame the gains as a property of the local weight neighborhood. In the following sections, we keep the PSV procedure fixed and vary only the perturbation space, asking whether the observed gains require perturbing the full weight vector. 4 Weight Perturbations Are Not Necessary We now investigate the mechanism underlying PSV. We progressively simplify the perturbation mechanism, first localizing it within the network and then moving it entirely to the output logits. This output-space view connects PSV to standard sampling, selection, and voting methods, allows us to isolate the source of its gains, and finally explains why internal perturbations behave similarly through the logit perturbations they induce. 4.1 Local Weight Perturbations Suffice Full-weight PSV, as used in Neural Thickets, perturbs every parameter of the model. However, such exhaustive perturbations are not necessary. On OLMo-3-7B-Instruct for Countdown with K = 50 K=50 , the greedy base model reaches 66.6 % 66.6\% and full-weight PSV reaches 90.8 % 90.8\% . Affiliation: Google DeepMind Loic Landrieu Affiliation: LIGM, CNRS, Univ Gustave Eiffel, ENPC, IP Paris Abstract The Neural Thickets hypothesis posits that pretrained language models lie in dense neighborhoods of task-specific experts in weight space, which random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. We reproduce the reported gains, but show that they do not require this geometric explanation. Perturbing a single decoder block already recovers much of the improvement, while keeping the model entirely frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks. This suggests an alternative explanation based on output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting. We formalize this view as Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), a general procedure that generates perturbed predictors, selects high-performing members on a small validation set, and aggregates their predictions. This interpretation connects Neural Thickets to established inference-time methods, including sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection. A first-order analysis further shows that small weight perturbations act primarily through their induced logit shifts. We extend this analysis to vision, where logit PSV substantially improves performance under domain shift, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations provide little additional benefit. Together, these results suggest that the gains attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead be obtained through output diversity, selection, and voting. Logit PSV realizes these benefits with a fully frozen model, providing a simple, training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision. Project page can be found here: https://kyutai.org/logit-psv . 1 Introduction Gan & Isola (2026) reported a striking phenomenon: randomly perturbing the weights of a pretrained language model can produce many variants that outperform it on specific reasoning tasks. The empirical gains are substantial, reaching up to 52.8 52.8 accuracy points (Countdown with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, from 10.8 % 10.8\% to 63.6 % 63.6\% ), and require little compute compared to fine-tuning. The authors propose a geometric explanation: pretrained weights of sufficiently large models are surrounded by a dense thicket of task-specialized models, recoverable by blind Gaussian perturbations. This paper first asks whether the gain requires perturbing the entire network. It does not: perturbing only a small fraction of the model, or even a single decoder block, recovers much of the gain. Pushing this observation to its limit, weight perturbations can be removed altogether: the model is kept completely frozen and only its output is perturbed: each member differs by a random Gaussian bias, fixed throughout autoregressive generation, added to the logits before greedy decoding. This logit-only variant performs no additional computation inside the network and modifies no model weight. Nevertheless, it recovers, and in some settings improves on, the gains of full-weight perturbations. On OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, it raises MATH-500 accuracy from 63.3 % 63.3\% to 81.3 % 81.3\% , compared with 74.7 % 74.7\% for the full-weight perturbation ensemble. Neural Thickets ( top ) perturb the full d 𝜽 d_{{\bm{\theta}}} -dimensional parameter vector, producing N N distinct networks. Logit PSV ( bottom ) keeps one frozen network and adds a V V -dimensional bias to the output logits, fixed across decoding steps and inputs. The Neural Thickets interpretation attributes these gains to local experts in weight space. Our experiments suggest a simpler account: perturbations induce output diversity, validation-based selection retains useful members, and voting aggregates their predictions. Neural Thickets can therefore be viewed as an instance of a broader perturb-select-vote (PSV) template: sample random perturbations, score the resulting members on a small validation set, retain the top K K , and vote at test time. This output-space view connects PSV to standard inference-time methods. A logit bias modifies the relative probability of each token, and greedy decoding under random biases defines a perturb-and-MAP sampler ( Papandreou & Yuille, 2011 ) . Selecting members by validation performance retains the biases that perform best on the target task, analogously to best-of- N N and verifier-guided selection ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , while voting relates PSV to self-consistency ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . A first-order analysis further supports this view: small weight perturbations act, to leading order, through the logit shifts they induce. This paper then isolates the roles of sampling, selection, and voting: on strong base models, temperature-tuned sampling with majority voting already matches full-weight PSV, showing that output diversity and ensembling explain most of the gain. On weaker models, validation-based selection remains important as it filters unreliable members before aggregation. Finally, the analysis extends to pretrained vision models under domain shift. In this setting, the analogue of a task expert is a domain expert: a perturbed representation that improves linear-probe performance on a target domain. Full-weight PSV, which perturbs the vision backbone and fits one probe per member, is compared to logit-only PSV, which fits a single probe and perturbs only the resulting class logits. The results support the same conclusion as in language: perturbing the logits is sufficient to recover the gains of full-weight perturbations, and often improves out-of-domain performance while leaving the backbone unchanged. Our results do not rule out useful structure in the neighborhood of pretrained weights. They show, however, that such structure is not required to obtain the observed gains. PSV is better understood as output diversification, validation-based filtering, and ensembling. Beyond its role in interpreting Neural Thickets, PSV yields a simple, training-free output-space procedure that substantially improves performance on specialized tasks and domains. Contributions. • Full-weight perturbations are unnecessary. Perturbing even a single decoder block recovers much of the gain of full-weight perturbations. • Logit PSV. Applying PSV directly to the output logits of a fully frozen model matches full-weight perturbation ensembles on reasoning tasks, and sometimes exceeds them. • An output-space interpretation of PSV. Perturbations induce output diversity, selection retains high-reward members, voting aggregates their predictions, and a first-order analysis connects weight perturbations to their induced logit shifts. • Extension to vision. Under domain shift, output-space perturbations recover the gains of full-weight perturbations for pretrained vision backbones as well. 2 Related Work Test-time sampling, selection, and voting. Inference-time scaling improves fixed models by generating multiple candidates and aggregating or selecting them. Self-consistency votes over sampled reasoning paths ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , while best-of- N N selects candidates using a verifier or reward model ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) ; more generally, increasing inference-time compute can substantially improve performance ( Snell et al., 2025 ) . Perturb-and-MAP provides a classical connection between perturbation and sampling, where random logit perturbations followed by MAP inference induce samples from a target distribution ( Papandreou & Yuille, 2011 ; Maddison et al., 2017 ) . Neural Thickets ( Gan & Isola, 2026 ) combines these ingredients: perturbations of the weights generate candidate models, validation performance selects them, and voting aggregates their predictions. Logit-space control. Many methods alter the behavior of a frozen model directly through its logits, including classifier-free guidance ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) , contrastive decoding ( Li et al., 2023 ) , post-hoc calibration ( Guo et al., 2017 ) , and watermarking, which biases a pseudo-random subset of token logits to embed a detectable signal ( Kirchenbauer et al., 2023 ) . These methods design or fit a particular logit transformation for a desired behavior. In contrast, logit PSV uses task-agnostic random biases and relies on selection and voting to exploit the resulting output diversity. Perturbations in weight space. Previous work has revealed substantial structure in the local geometry of neural-network parameters, including mode connectivity ( Garipov et al., 2018 ) , model averaging ( Izmailov et al., 2018 ; Wortsman et al., 2022 ) , and low-dimensional adaptation ( Li et al., 2018 ; Hu et al., 2022 ) . Random weight perturbations are also central to evolution strategies and zeroth-order optimization ( Salimans et al., 2017 ) . Our focus is different: rather than optimizing or merging perturbations, we ask which aspects of weight-space perturbation are actually necessary for the gains of PSV. items.content: world2vec: Mechanistic world models through latent dynamics learning Tobias Schmidt † † thanks: Equal contribution $ ˆ†$ Correspondence to steffen.schneider@helmholtz-munich.de Rodrigo Gonzalez Laiz † † footnotemark: Krisztián Szuppinger & Steffen Schneider † Helmholtz Munich & Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML) Abstract World models can achieve strong control performance without faithfully capturing the dynamics of their environment, limiting their potential for mechanistic interpretability and scientific discovery. Here, we introduce world2vec to learn mechanistic world models without reward information directly from observations and actions. World2vec learns latent dynamics that faithfully reproduce the true system over long prediction horizons, with at least one order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2 and LeWM. This enables state of the art performance in controlling continuous environments from pixels and accurate system identification across a benchmark of 71 attractors, demonstrating how world models are amenable to scientific discovery. https://worldmodels.science 1 Introduction Estimating models of dynamically changing systems and environments is an important problem at the frontier of representation learning, with applications in physical AI and scientific discovery may1976simple , ha2018world , ha2018recurrent , course2023state , mathis2026joint , lecun2022jepa , schmidhuber1990making . Here we focus on the problem where a state 𝒔 {\bm{s}} evolves under actions 𝒂 {\bm{a}} according to dynamics 𝐟 {\mathbf{f}} , and we observe this state through a non-linear mixing function 𝐠 {\mathbf{g}} : 𝒔 ˙ = 𝐟 ⁡ ( 𝒔 , 𝒂 ) , 𝒙 = 𝐠 ⁡ ( 𝒔 ) . \dot{{\bm{s}}}={\mathbf{f}}({\bm{s}},{\bm{a}}),\qquad{\bm{x}}={\mathbf{g}}({\bm{s}}). (1) Then, latent world modeling lecun2022jepa is the problem of jointly estimating, from observations and actions alone, an encoder 𝐡 {\mathbf{h}} that maps observations to a representation 𝒛 = 𝐡 ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) {\bm{z}}={\mathbf{h}}({\bm{x}}) and a latent dynamics model 𝐟 ^ \hat{\mathbf{f}} that describes how this representation evolves in time. Ideally, the representation is a change of coordinates of the state, 𝒛 = 𝐫 ⁡ ( 𝒔 ) {\bm{z}}={\mathbf{r}}({\bm{s}}) with 𝐫 = 𝐡 ∘ 𝐠 {\mathbf{r}}={\mathbf{h}}\circ{\mathbf{g}} invertible, and the latent dynamics reproduce the true evolution in these coordinates laiz2026understanding , 𝒛 ˙ = 𝐟 ^ ( 𝒛 , 𝒂 ) , 𝒛 ( 0 ) = 𝐫 ( 𝒔 ( 0 ) ) ⟹ 𝒛 ( t ) = 𝐫 ( 𝒔 ( t ) ) for all t ≥ 0 . \dot{{\bm{z}}}=\hat{\mathbf{f}}({\bm{z}},{\bm{a}}),\quad{\bm{z}}(0)={\mathbf{r}}({\bm{s}}(0))\quad\Longrightarrow\quad{\bm{z}}(t)={\mathbf{r}}({\bm{s}}(t))\ \ \text{for all }t\geq 0. (2) If this condition holds, the world model ( 𝐡 , 𝐟 ^ ) ({\mathbf{h}},\hat{\mathbf{f}}) can support model-predictive control or model-based reinforcement learning to steer the environment into desired target states. Over the past years, this type of world modeling has become feasible and gained theoretical grounding. Common objectives are reconstruction-based forecasting dreamer , reconstruction-free planning in latent space, either trained with rewards burchi2025learning , tdmpc2 or reward-free using the joint-embedding predictive architecture lecun2022jepa , lewm , zhou2024dino (JEPA). Figure 1 : A. World2vec jointly learns representations and dynamics in latent space; the dynamics model is an action-conditioned neural ODE which can be parameterized to provide an interpretable vector representation of the dynamics. The objective function incorporates assumptions about the underlying data-generating process. B. Reward vs. 1 s Equivariance Accuracy (EQA) of world2vec vs. baselines, averaged across environments. Importantly, world modeling extends beyond solving a particular control task. We also seek to ensure that the world model accurately reflects the world in a statistical sense: Does the learned dynamics model reproduce the relevant dynamics when the statistical assumptions used to build it are satisfied? If satisfied, an appropriate parameterization can further enable mechanistic interpretability by allowing us to read out the environmental dynamics. This has value both for interpretability and scientific applications. World models with these properties have recently been characterized as mechanistic world models mech_world_models . Building on ideas from non-linear independent component analysis pmlr-v89-hyvarinen19a , it has been shown that self-supervised learning is able to provably estimate latent representations and their dynamics from data dcl across a range of objective functions. mikulasch2026understanding , mikulasch2026predictive Transferring these theoretical guarantees into algorithms that scale to challenging control problems is the goal of this present work. In this paper, we propose world2vec ( Fig. 1 A) to advance the shared goal of building a world model that ( i ) achieves state-of-the-art performance on control tasks after training on offline data alone, ( ii ) faithfully models the environment, measured via long-range rollouts and predictions, and ( iii ) is mechanistically interpretable and thus suitable for scientific applications. World2vec is agnostic to its exact training objective, provided it belongs to a class of objectives known to yield identifiable representations under idealized conditions. We consider LeJEPA lejepa , lewm and dynamics contrastive learning dcl (DCL) as two possible approaches to achieving this goal. These objectives encode statistical assumptions with different implications on numerical estimation, and an increasing body of theoretical work addresses the identifiability of these objectives zimmermann_contrastive_2021 , dcl , lejepa_identifiability , mikulasch2026understanding . Across three considered environments, world2vec jointly achieves high reward and performance in forecasting ( Fig. 1 B), enabling successful model predictive control in 2 of 3 environments, none of which were solvable by the previous best JEPA-based approach lewm . In the remainder of the paper, we introduce the idea of dynamics matching and the world2vec framework ( § 2 ), which we benchmark on control across several MuJoCo environments ( § 3 ) and on symbolic regression ( ). 2 The world2vec framework for mechanistic world modeling Mechanistic world modeling mech_world_models seeks to recover a representation of the physical state, a faithful model of its evolution, and ideally an interpretable description of the governing equations. For the system in Eq. 1 , we observe 𝒙 {\bm{x}} and 𝒂 {\bm{a}} , but have no direct access to 𝒔 {\bm{s}} or 𝐟 {\mathbf{f}} . We aim to learn an encoder 𝐡 {\mathbf{h}} that maps observations to latent states 𝒛 = 𝐡 ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) {\bm{z}}={\mathbf{h}}({\bm{x}}) , and their dynamics 𝒛 ˙ = 𝐟 ^ ​ ( 𝒛 , 𝒂 ) \dot{{\bm{z}}}=\hat{\mathbf{f}}({\bm{z}},{\bm{a}}) . Faithful latent dynamics. When does this learned model faithfully describe the physical system? Let 𝐫 = 𝐡 ∘ 𝐠 {\mathbf{r}}={\mathbf{h}}\circ{\mathbf{g}} denote the mapping from physical to latent states. If 𝐫 {\mathbf{r}} is invertible, the latent representation is simply a change of coordinates of the physical state. The model is then faithful laiz2026understanding if encoding the evolved physical state yields the same trajectory as evolving the encoded state in latent space ( Eq. 2 ). Integrating the latent dynamics over a horizon T T , we require: 𝒛 ^ t ​ ( T ) := 𝒛 ⁡ ( t ) + ∫ 0 T 𝐟 ^ ​ ( 𝒛 ^ t ​ ( τ ) , 𝒂 ⁡ ( t + τ ) ) ​ 𝑑 τ ​ = ! ​ 𝐡 ​ ( 𝒙 ⁡ ( t + T ) ) for all ​ t , T ≥ 0 . \hat{\bm{z}}_{t}(T):={\bm{z}}(t)+\int_{0}^{T}\hat{\mathbf{f}}\big(\hat{\bm{z}}_{t}(\tau),{\bm{a}}(t+\tau)\big)\,d\tau\overset{!}{=}{\mathbf{h}}\big({\bm{x}}(t+T)\big)\qquad\text{for all }t,\ T\geq 0. (3) Importantly, both sides of this condition can be computed from observations and actions alone, without access to the states 𝒔 {\bm{s}} or the ground truth dynamics 𝐟 {\mathbf{f}} . The world2vec objective. To learn the encoder–dynamics pair ( 𝐡 , 𝐟 ^ ) ({\mathbf{h}},\hat{\mathbf{f}}) in practice, we collect a dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} with observations sampled at intervals Δ ​ t \Delta t , i.e., at times t n = n ​ Δ ​ t t_{n}=n\Delta t , and recorded actions. Under partial observability, a single observation does not necessarily determine the state; for example, velocities cannot be inferred from a single frame. The world2vec algorithm is a numerical implementation of learning principles that have been extensively studied theoretically and are known to produce representations that are consistent up to at least affine transformations zimmermann_contrastive_2021 , mikulasch2026understanding , lejepa_identifiability . The challenge lies in the numerical estimation to obtain this guarantee in practice. As an empirical measure of identifiability, we check whether independently trained encoders recover equivalent representations up to an affine change of coordinates, termed consistency schneider2023cebra . The controller executes a prefix of the selected plan and replans from newly observed data, using neither a learned reward model nor a state decoder. 3 Faithful dynamics modeling for continuous control 3.1 Experimental Setup Figure 2 : Pendulum, Reacher and CartPole environments used in our study with their physical variables. Environments and dataset collection. We evaluate world2vec on the Pendulum, Reacher, and Cartpole environments from the MuJoCo-based DeepMind Control Suite control_suite ( Fig. 2 ). We collect 200k RGB frames with 64 × \times 64 px resolution using random policies in each environment: uniform random actions for Reacher, and temporally correlated Ornstein–Uhlenbeck actions for Pendulum and Cartpole (details in ). For identifiability analysis, we construct a variant of this dataset with non-visual, non-linear observations. Following dcl , the positional and angular coordinates (but not velocities) are passed through a randomly initialized, injective MLP of varying depth and projected to 50 dimensions. Model families and training. Encoders take a short sequence of H = 3 H=3 observations as input. A small vision transformer encodes each frame (16 × \times 16 patches, 2 layers of width 64 with 4 heads, and a keypoint readout) and is followed by an MLP head (2 hidden layers of 128 units) that maps the sequence of frame representations to the latent state. On nonlinear-mixing observations, we concatenate the observation sequence and pass it through an MLP encoder (3 hidden layers of 128 units). Dynamics models are MLPs with 3 hidden layers of 128 units. To model continuous-time dynamics, the MLP parametrizes the vector field 𝐟 ^ \hat{\mathbf{f}} and 𝚽 {\bm{\Phi}} is one Euler step ( Eq. 5 ). As a baseline close to existing JEPA-setups, we parameterize discrete-time dynamics by replacing the Euler step ( Eq. 5 ) with 𝚽 ⁡ ( 𝒛 , 𝒂 ) = MLP ⁡ ( 𝒛 , 𝒂 ) {\bm{\Phi}}({\bm{z}},{\bm{a}})=\mathrm{MLP}({\bm{z}},{\bm{a}}) , where the MLP directly predicts the next latent state. With a latent dimensionality of d = 32 d=32 , the main world2vec model has 263k parameters (221k for the encoder, 42k for the dynamics). All models are trained for 20k iterations with Adam using learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} and cosine decay. Model predictive control. We control the environments with model predictive control (MPC) in latent space without access to reward. Instead, we assume knowledge of an observation sequence that shows the desired target. We encode this sequence to obtain a goal latent that describes which part of the latent space the environment should be driven towards. For Pendulum and Cartpole, this is a sequence of frames that show the pole or pendulum upright at rest, with the cart centered. For Reacher, the target changes in every episode, and the goal is underspecified since two arm configurations place the fingertip on the target. We therefore compute, per episode, the arm configuration that places the fingertip on the target via inverse kinematics, render it, and use its encoding as the goal. Both possible elbow configurations are planned and the average between them is reported. We then sample candidate action sequences using the cross-entropy method rubinstein1999cross (CEM), predict future latent states with the dynamics model and rank them via their distance to the goal state ( Eq. 12 ). We execute the first actions of the best sequence, observe the environment, and plan again. Because the continuous-time dynamics can be integrated with a different step size, it is possible to use different sampling rates for training and testing. Baselines and Metrics. TD-MPC2 and DreamerV3 are trained online following their respective training protocols. LeWM and world2vec are trained offline on a random-policy dataset . For Reacher, we report LeWM trained on the original LeWM dataset lewm in the main results and compare it with LeWM trained on our dataset in . All models are evaluated on the same held-out test episodes of our datasets. As a controlled baseline within our own framework, we implement a LeWM variant using discrete dynamics, one-step prediction, and the SIGReg regularizer. This baseline has similar performance to LeWM in terms of LRC and EQA and is substantially faster due to a more compact model. We measure the quality of the representation through consistency and the quality of the rollout using LRC and EQA as detailed in § 2 . Hyperparameters are selected using the highest mean validation EQA on the validation split. We measure task performance via cumulative reward. All metrics are outlined in detail in . Implementation. We implemented world2vec in PyTorch. For the considered control tasks, small models with 64 × \times 64 px frame inputs are sufficient, while the framework allows encoders with larger inputs. On a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, training takes only 2–6 minutes for a one-step model, about 10 minutes for a 20-step model, and about 30 minutes for a 40-step model. Closed-loop control takes about 20–50 ms per control step, including simulation and rendering. Beyond empirical performance, this efficiency enables downstream applications in robotics and closed-loop experimental settings. 3.2 Results Table 1 : Consistency, LRC and EQA (%) on the test split, averaged over environments, and reward per environment (maximum 1000; best planner per environment). Mean ± \pm bootstrap standard error over model seeds; best in bold, second-best underlined. On Reacher, the baselines and world2vec run at 8.3 Hz, TD-MPC2 and DreamerV3 at 25 Hz, and LeWM, trained on the original LeWM data, at 5 Hz (see and for details on hyperparameters).
items.raw_text: world2vec: Mechanistic world models through latent dynamics learning Tobias Schmidt † † thanks: Equal contribution $ ˆ†$ Correspondence to steffen.schneider@helmholtz-munich.de Rodrigo Gonzalez Laiz † † footnotemark: Krisztián Szuppinger & Steffen Schneider † Helmholtz Munich & Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML) Abstract World models can achieve strong control performance without faithfully capturing the dynamics of their environment, limiting their potential for mechanistic interpretability and scientific discovery. Here, we introduce world2vec to learn mechanistic world models without reward information directly from observations and actions. World2vec learns latent dynamics that faithfully reproduce the true system over long prediction horizons, with at least one order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2 and LeWM. This enables state of the art performance in controlling continuous environments from pixels and accurate system identification across a benchmark of 71 attractors, demonstrating how world models are amenable to scientific discovery. https://worldmodels.science 1 Introduction Estimating models of dynamically changing systems and environments is an important problem at the frontier of representation learning, with applications in physical AI and scientific discovery may1976simple , ha2018world , ha2018recurrent , course2023state , mathis2026joint , lecun2022jepa , schmidhuber1990making . Here we focus on the problem where a state 𝒔 {\bm{s}} evolves under actions 𝒂 {\bm{a}} according to dynamics 𝐟 {\mathbf{f}} , and we observe this state through a non-linear mixing function 𝐠 {\mathbf{g}} : 𝒔 ˙ = 𝐟 ⁡ ( 𝒔 , 𝒂 ) , 𝒙 = 𝐠 ⁡ ( 𝒔 ) . \dot{{\bm{s}}}={\mathbf{f}}({\bm{s}},{\bm{a}}),\qquad{\bm{x}}={\mathbf{g}}({\bm{s}}). Ideally, the representation is a change of coordinates of the state, 𝒛 = 𝐫 ⁡ ( 𝒔 ) {\bm{z}}={\mathbf{r}}({\bm{s}}) with 𝐫 = 𝐡 ∘ 𝐠 {\mathbf{r}}={\mathbf{h}}\circ{\mathbf{g}} invertible, and the latent dynamics reproduce the true evolution in these coordinates laiz2026understanding , 𝒛 ˙ = 𝐟 ^ ( 𝒛 , 𝒂 ) , 𝒛 ( 0 ) = 𝐫 ( 𝒔 ( 0 ) ) ⟹ 𝒛 ( t ) = 𝐫 ( 𝒔 ( t ) ) for all t ≥ 0 . \dot{{\bm{z}}}=\hat{\mathbf{f}}({\bm{z}},{\bm{a}}),\quad{\bm{z}}(0)={\mathbf{r}}({\bm{s}}(0))\quad\Longrightarrow\quad{\bm{z}}(t)={\mathbf{r}}({\bm{s}}(t))\ \ \text{for all }t\geq 0. (2) If this condition holds, the world model ( 𝐡 , 𝐟 ^ ) ({\mathbf{h}},\hat{\mathbf{f}}) can support model-predictive control or model-based reinforcement learning to steer the environment into desired target states. Over the past years, this type of world modeling has become feasible and gained theoretical grounding. Common objectives are reconstruction-based forecasting dreamer , reconstruction-free planning in latent space, either trained with rewards burchi2025learning , tdmpc2 or reward-free using the joint-embedding predictive architecture lecun2022jepa , lewm , zhou2024dino (JEPA). Figure 1 : A. World2vec jointly learns representations and dynamics in latent space; the dynamics model is an action-conditioned neural ODE which can be parameterized to provide an interpretable vector representation of the dynamics. The objective function incorporates assumptions about the underlying data-generating process. B. Reward vs. 1 s Equivariance Accuracy (EQA) of world2vec vs. baselines, averaged across environments. Importantly, world modeling extends beyond solving a particular control task. We also seek to ensure that the world model accurately reflects the world in a statistical sense: Does the learned dynamics model reproduce the relevant dynamics when the statistical assumptions used to build it are satisfied? If satisfied, an appropriate parameterization can further enable mechanistic interpretability by allowing us to read out the environmental dynamics. This has value both for interpretability and scientific applications. World models with these properties have recently been characterized as mechanistic world models mech_world_models . Building on ideas from non-linear independent component analysis pmlr-v89-hyvarinen19a , it has been shown that self-supervised learning is able to provably estimate latent representations and their dynamics from data dcl across a range of objective functions. mikulasch2026understanding , mikulasch2026predictive Transferring these theoretical guarantees into algorithms that scale to challenging control problems is the goal of this present work. In this paper, we propose world2vec ( Fig. 1 A) to advance the shared goal of building a world model that ( i ) achieves state-of-the-art performance on control tasks after training on offline data alone, ( ii ) faithfully models the environment, measured via long-range rollouts and predictions, and ( iii ) is mechanistically interpretable and thus suitable for scientific applications. World2vec is agnostic to its exact training objective, provided it belongs to a class of objectives known to yield identifiable representations under idealized conditions. We consider LeJEPA lejepa , lewm and dynamics contrastive learning dcl (DCL) as two possible approaches to achieving this goal. These objectives encode statistical assumptions with different implications on numerical estimation, and an increasing body of theoretical work addresses the identifiability of these objectives zimmermann_contrastive_2021 , dcl , lejepa_identifiability , mikulasch2026understanding . Across three considered environments, world2vec jointly achieves high reward and performance in forecasting ( Fig. 1 B), enabling successful model predictive control in 2 of 3 environments, none of which were solvable by the previous best JEPA-based approach lewm . The world2vec algorithm is a numerical implementation of learning principles that have been extensively studied theoretically and are known to produce representations that are consistent up to at least affine transformations zimmermann_contrastive_2021 , mikulasch2026understanding , lejepa_identifiability . The challenge lies in the numerical estimation to obtain this guarantee in practice. As an empirical measure of identifiability, we check whether independently trained encoders recover equivalent representations up to an affine change of coordinates, termed consistency schneider2023cebra . To estimate consistency, we report the R 2 R^{2} after optimal affine alignment for the two encoders 𝐡 1 {\mathbf{h}}_{1} and 𝐡 2 {\mathbf{h}}_{2} , max 𝑳 , 𝒃 ⁡ R 2 ​ [ { 𝐡 2 ​ ( 𝑿 n ) } n , { 𝑳 ​ 𝐡 1 ​ ( 𝑿 n ) + 𝒃 } n ] , \max_{{\bm{L}},{\bm{b}}}R^{2}\left[\{{\mathbf{h}}_{2}({\bm{X}}_{n})\}_{n},\{{\bm{L}}{\mathbf{h}}_{1}({\bm{X}}_{n})+{\bm{b}}\}_{n}\right], (9) across independent training runs. This score compares predictions and encoded futures from the same encoder–dynamics pair, but can be prone to collapse (i.e., a trivial embedding could get a high LRC). Hence, we also adopt the accuracy-based equivariance measure of schmidt2025ebc which for our time series case we denote as Equivariance Accuracy (EQA). EQA is the top-1 retrieval accuracy of the encoded future observation among negative candidates. We select model hyperparameters based on validation EQA and use 512 negatives in all experiments. Dynamics parameterization. The function class for 𝐟 ^ \hat{{\mathbf{f}}} can be flexibly chosen within the world2vec framework. For our main experiments focused on control, we utilize an MLP that maps latent state and action to the rate of change. As a more interpretable parameterization, we build on SINDy sindy and the more recent DYSCO dysco and fit the structured dynamics model 𝐟 ^ ​ ( 𝒛 , 𝒂 ) = 𝚵 ​ 𝜽 ​ ( 𝒛 , 𝒂 ) , \hat{{\mathbf{f}}}({\bm{z}},{\bm{a}})=\bm{\Xi}\,\bm{\theta}({\bm{z}},{\bm{a}}), (11) where 𝜽 ⁡ ( 𝒛 , 𝒂 ) ∈ ℝ p \bm{\theta}({\bm{z}},{\bm{a}})\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is a fixed vector of library features and 𝚵 ∈ ℝ d × p \bm{\Xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times p} contains learned coefficients for a d d -dimensional latent space. Our SINDy instantiation uses polynomial features for 𝜽 \bm{\theta} and an L 1 L_{1} penalty on 𝚵 \bm{\Xi} sindy , sindy_ae , sindy_bae . Model-predictive control. Given a sequence of target frames 𝑿 ⋆ {\bm{X}}^{\star} , we define 𝒛 ⋆ = 𝐡 ⁡ ( 𝑿 ⋆ ) {\bm{z}}^{\star}={\mathbf{h}}({\bm{X}}^{\star}) as the goal state. Starting from the current history 𝑿 n {\bm{X}}_{n} , we sample candidate action sequences of planning horizon P P with the cross-entropy method rubinstein1999cross (CEM) using the rollout in Eq. 4 and minimize min 𝒂 n : n + P − 1 ∑ j = 1 P β j ∥ 𝒛 ^ n , j − 𝒛 ⋆ ∥ 2 2 , s.t. β j ≥ 0 , ∑ j = 1 P β j = 1 , \min_{{\bm{a}}_{n:n+P-1}}\sum_{j=1}^{P}\beta_{j}\|\hat{{\bm{z}}}_{n,j}-{\bm{z}}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\text{ s.t. }\beta_{j}\geq 0,\quad\sum_{j=1}^{P}\beta_{j}=1, (12) subject to the environment’s action bounds. The controller executes a prefix of the selected plan and replans from newly observed data, using neither a learned reward model nor a state decoder. 3 Faithful dynamics modeling for continuous control 3.1 Experimental Setup Figure 2 : Pendulum, Reacher and CartPole environments used in our study with their physical variables. Environments and dataset collection. We evaluate world2vec on the Pendulum, Reacher, and Cartpole environments from the MuJoCo-based DeepMind Control Suite control_suite ( Fig. 2 ). We collect 200k RGB frames with 64 × \times 64 px resolution using random policies in each environment: uniform random actions for Reacher, and temporally correlated Ornstein–Uhlenbeck actions for Pendulum and Cartpole (details in ). For identifiability analysis, we construct a variant of this dataset with non-visual, non-linear observations. Following dcl , the positional and angular coordinates (but not velocities) are passed through a randomly initialized, injective MLP of varying depth and projected to 50 dimensions. Model families and training. Encoders take a short sequence of H = 3 H=3 observations as input. A small vision transformer encodes each frame (16 × \times 16 patches, 2 layers of width 64 with 4 heads, and a keypoint readout) and is followed by an MLP head (2 hidden layers of 128 units) that maps the sequence of frame representations to the latent state. On nonlinear-mixing observations, we concatenate the observation sequence and pass it through an MLP encoder (3 hidden layers of 128 units). Dynamics models are MLPs with 3 hidden layers of 128 units. To model continuous-time dynamics, the MLP parametrizes the vector field 𝐟 ^ \hat{\mathbf{f}} and 𝚽 {\bm{\Phi}} is one Euler step ( Eq. 5 ). As a baseline close to existing JEPA-setups, we parameterize discrete-time dynamics by replacing the Euler step ( Eq. 5 ) with 𝚽 ⁡ ( 𝒛 , 𝒂 ) = MLP ⁡ ( 𝒛 , 𝒂 ) {\bm{\Phi}}({\bm{z}},{\bm{a}})=\mathrm{MLP}({\bm{z}},{\bm{a}}) , where the MLP directly predicts the next latent state. With a latent dimensionality of d = 32 d=32 , the main world2vec model has 263k parameters (221k for the encoder, 42k for the dynamics). All models are trained for 20k iterations with Adam using learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} and cosine decay. Model predictive control. We control the environments with model predictive control (MPC) in latent space without access to reward. Instead, we assume knowledge of an observation sequence that shows the desired target. We encode this sequence to obtain a goal latent that describes which part of the latent space the environment should be driven towards. For Pendulum and Cartpole, this is a sequence of frames that show the pole or pendulum upright at rest, with the cart centered. For Reacher, the target changes in every episode, and the goal is underspecified since two arm configurations place the fingertip on the target. We therefore compute, per episode, the arm configuration that places the fingertip on the target via inverse kinematics, render it, and use its encoding as the goal. Both possible elbow configurations are planned and the average between them is reported. We then sample candidate action sequences using the cross-entropy method rubinstein1999cross (CEM), predict future latent states with the dynamics model and rank them via their distance to the goal state ( Eq. 12 ). We execute the first actions of the best sequence, observe the environment, and plan again. Because the continuous-time dynamics can be integrated with a different step size, it is possible to use different sampling rates for training and testing. Baselines and Metrics. TD-MPC2 and DreamerV3 are trained online following their respective training protocols. LeWM and world2vec are trained offline on a random-policy dataset . For Reacher, we report LeWM trained on the original LeWM dataset lewm in the main results and compare it with LeWM trained on our dataset in . All models are evaluated on the same held-out test episodes of our datasets. As a controlled baseline within our own framework, we implement a LeWM variant using discrete dynamics, one-step prediction, and the SIGReg regularizer. This baseline has similar performance to LeWM in terms of LRC and EQA and is substantially faster due to a more compact model. We measure the quality of the representation through consistency and the quality of the rollout using LRC and EQA as detailed in § 2 . Hyperparameters are selected using the highest mean validation EQA on the validation split. We measure task performance via cumulative reward. All metrics are outlined in detail in . Implementation. We implemented world2vec in PyTorch. For the considered control tasks, small models with 64 × \times 64 px frame inputs are sufficient, while the framework allows encoders with larger inputs. On a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, training takes only 2–6 minutes for a one-step model, about 10 minutes for a 20-step model, and about 30 minutes for a 40-step model. Closed-loop control takes about 20–50 ms per control step, including simulation and rendering. Beyond empirical performance, this efficiency enables downstream applications in robotics and closed-loop experimental settings. 3.2 Results Table 1 : Consistency, LRC and EQA (%) on the test split, averaged over environments, and reward per environment (maximum 1000; best planner per environment). Mean ± \pm bootstrap standard error over model seeds; best in bold, second-best underlined. On Reacher, the baselines and world2vec run at 8.3 Hz, TD-MPC2 and DreamerV3 at 25 Hz, and LeWM, trained on the original LeWM data, at 5 Hz (see and for details on hyperparameters).

items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.40618 (cs) [Submitted on 29 Oct 2026] Title: An ODE-based Sampler for Discrete Diffusion Models Authors: Samson Gourevitch , Yazid Janati , Eric Moulines , Eric P. Xing , Alain Durmus , Giacomo Zanella View a PDF of the paper titled An ODE-based Sampler for Discrete Diffusion Models, by Samson Gourevitch and 5 other authors View PDF Abstract: The marginals of a continuous diffusion model can be reproduced by a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), known as the probability flow ODE, which provides a foundation for accelerated sampling and consistency distillation. In this paper we address the question whether an analogous formulation exists for discrete diffusion models and answer it affirmatively by introducing exponential residual flows (ERFs). Our framework augments the discrete state with a continuous residual variable for each token and position. These residuals evolve deterministically according to piecewise-defined ODEs whose vector fields depend on the current discrete state and the forward and backward rate matrices of the prescribed diffusion model. The discrete state changes whenever a residual reaches zero. We prove that this construction preserves the marginals of the original diffusion. We derive a practical discretization of our sampler and specialize it to masked and uniform diffusion. The deterministic trajectories of ERFs support consistency distillation and yield empirical improvements over previous approaches across a variety of benchmarks including code and text generation tasks. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.40564 (cs) [Submitted on 29 Oct 2026] Title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm Authors: Yuda Song , Alvin Zhang , Fahim Tajwar , Daman Arora , Jeff Schneider , Daniel Khashabi , Ruslan Salakhutdinov , J. Andrew Bagnell , Aarti Singh , Andrea Zanette View a PDF of the paper titled Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm, by Yuda Song and 9 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm, unified training. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities, and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.40589 (cs) [Submitted on 29 Oct 2026] Title: Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins Authors: El Mustapha Mansouri , Eikichi Kimura , Masato Koga , Keigo Arai View a PDF of the paper titled Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins, by El Mustapha Mansouri and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: An autonomous research laboratory could conduct an entire study, from formulating questions to preparing manuscripts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers one route towards this goal. Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which agents based on large language models assess one another's work and can stop or redirect investigations. They can generate and reject research questions, require separate theoretical checks and conduct experiments designed to challenge their claims. We demonstrate these capabilities by investigating ensembles of quantum spins in diamond. The agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a defined family of microwave pulse sequences. They checked the result computationally and designed experiments to distinguish competing predictions. An initial experiment agreed with the theoretical predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions. This study demonstrates that collaborating AI agents can select research questions, derive theoretical results and test their predictions experimentally. Comments: 17 pages, 5 figures. items.content: Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins El Mustapha Mansouri * Eikichi Kimura Masato Koga Keigo Arai † Affiliation: School of Engineering, Institute of Science Tokyo, Yokohama, Kanagawa 226-8501, Japan 29 October 2026 Abstract An autonomous research laboratory could conduct an entire study, from formulating questions to preparing manuscripts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers one route towards this goal. Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which agents based on large language models assess one another’s work and can stop or redirect investigations. They can generate and reject research questions, require separate theoretical checks and conduct experiments designed to challenge their claims. We demonstrate these capabilities by investigating ensembles of quantum spins in diamond. The agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a defined family of microwave pulse sequences. They checked the result computationally and designed experiments to distinguish competing predictions. An initial experiment agreed with the theoretical predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions. This study demonstrates that collaborating AI agents can select research questions, derive theoretical results and test their predictions experimentally. 1 1 footnotetext: Corresponding author: mansouri.e.2224@m.isct.ac.jp 2 2 footnotetext: Corresponding author: arai.k.835f@m.isct.ac.jp To conduct research autonomously, a system must decide what to investigate, how to test its ideas and what to conclude from the results. Robot scientists have generated hypotheses and tested them in the laboratory [ 1 , 2 ] , while autonomous laboratories have used experimental feedback to select and carry out further experiments [ 3 , 4 ] . Systems based on large language models (LLMs) can also search the literature, propose ideas, plan experiments and analyse data [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . In recent studies, LLMs have challenged hypotheses, checked physical reasoning and revised interpretations in response to experimental evidence [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 6 ] . A demanding test is whether agents can use this criticism to guide a study in which they develop a theoretical claim and design experiments to test it. Agents may complete every step of a study yet still draw a conclusion that the evidence does not support. In one evaluation, an AI Scientist reported performance improvements that were based on flawed experiments [ 11 ] . We therefore ask whether agents can revise their experiments or conclusions when criticism reveals a flaw. Scientific judgement becomes most consequential when it prevents an apparently promising investigation from proceeding. A plausible research question may already have an answer, and an elegant mathematical argument may rest on an unchecked assumption. For a proposed physical law, even a rigorous mathematical derivation cannot establish its empirical validity and relevance: its predictions must also withstand experiments designed to distinguish them from competing explanations. Organized scepticism requires these uncertainties to be confronted rather than merely acknowledged [ 12 ] . Independent verification, precommitted predictions and acceptance criteria, and experimental controls provide safeguards against unjustified conclusions [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] . The critical test is whether AI agents can enforce these safeguards, even when doing so means rejecting their own work. Ensembles of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond provide a suitable setting for this test. Their optically readable spins can be manipulated through precisely controlled microwave-pulse sequences, while variations in spin properties create a nontrivial problem of predicting ensemble responses [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] . This combination of experimental control and physical complexity allows mathematical predictions to be independently examined and tested against simpler calibration methods. The platform thus provides an opportunity to evaluate whether AI agents can formulate a meaningful question, establish a theoretical result and design an experiment capable of challenging that result rather than merely confirming it. Here we present a collaborative AI laboratory that uses scientific criticism to guide an investigation from question selection to experimental assessment. Our objective is to determine whether collaborating agents can develop a substantive theoretical result and establish what experimental evidence supports its predictions. The agents pursued this objective by identifying the minimum calibration information needed to predict unmeasured responses of an NV spin ensemble, without reconstructing the unknown distribution of spin errors. The transition from theory to experiment required further collaboration: an experimentalist agent developed the control software and performed measurements, while a manager agent proposed redesigning the experiment rather than stopping after an agent serving as principal investigator rejected an initial design. During the research an experiment failed, the agents investigated the discrepancy and revised the acquisition procedure. The final measurements supported the calibration law developed by the proposer and PI. Together, the mathematical result and its experimental test demonstrate a scientific investigation in which AI agents collectively selected, challenged and substantiated a new physical claim. 1 Collaborative AI laboratory for scientific discovery To investigate whether scientific judgement can emerge through collaboration among AI agents, we developed a research system that distributes scientific responsibilities across specialized agents (Fig. 1 ). The system connects research-question generation, theoretical analysis, computational verification and physical experimentation through exchanges of research outputs and critical feedback. Rather than automatically advancing results from one stage to the next, agents evaluate the work of their collaborators and can reject or request revisions when scientific criteria are not satisfied. By separating the generation and evaluation of scientific claims across agents with distinct contexts, this design aims to reduce self-confirmation bias and the reinforcement of erroneous assumptions across successive reasoning steps [ 19 , 20 ] . The laboratory comprised six principal agent roles: proposers, a principal investigator (PI), a computational researcher, an experimentalist, a manager and independent reviewers (Fig. 1 ). The proposers independently generated candidate research questions, which the PI evaluated for scientific novelty, logical consistency, significance and experimental feasibility. After selecting a research question, the PI developed its theoretical foundations, while the computational researcher independently verified the mathematical results and examined the robustness of their underlying assumptions on a supercomputer. The experimentalist developed the instrument-control software and performed measurements on an NV-diamond platform. The manager coordinated exchanges between the agents and contributed to experimental planning, while independent reviewers assessed the resulting manuscript. Scientific evaluation was integrated into the communication between agents rather than restricted to a final review. Research outputs were exchanged through written documents, and key decisions required explicit assessments before the investigation could proceed (Fig. 1 ). Rejected proposals could be revised in response to criticism, mathematical claims were subjected to independent verification, and experimental designs could be reconsidered when they failed to distinguish the proposed theory from alternative explanations. Experimental predictions and acceptance criteria were fixed before the target measurements were analysed. These mechanisms allowed criticism to influence not only the interpretation of results, but also the direction and execution of the research itself. Human researchers assembled the apparatus and configured the safety agent with preset operating limits. Within these boundaries, the AI agents carried out the calibration investigation through their respective roles, from research-question selection to experimental assessment. Figure 1: Scientific workflow and coordination of the collaborative AI laboratory. (a) Five-stage research cycle with checkpoints overseen by the principal investigator (PI). Dotted lines indicate PI involvement; dashed arrows indicate rejection and revision. (b) Specialized AI agents and their exchanges of research outputs, with safety-agent approval required before experimentation. (c) Document flow during one pass through the API-orchestrated workflow, from left to right (not to scale). The orchestrator routes documents to the persistent PI conversation (blue). Dots mark document deliveries, circled ticks and crosses indicate PI decisions, and dashed links trace rejected work. Upper branches represent separate model calls; lower blocks represent coding-agent jobs. 2 Critical evaluation and selection of research questions We first examined how the laboratory selected a research question from independently generated proposals (Fig. 2 ). Each proposer received a description of the experimental platform and was tasked with identifying a mathematically substantive research question in machine learning or information science in which physics was essential, without access to the other proposals. The principal-investigator (PI) agent evaluated the proposals in batches, assessing their scientific novelty, logical validity, significance and experimental feasibility. Rather than selecting the most promising candidate by default, the PI could reject an entire batch and provide written criticism to guide subsequent proposals. This selectivity proved consequential. Over approximately 30 hours, the PI rejected 75 proposals, accepting none during the first 17 batches (Fig. 2 a,b). The rejections reflected recurring problems: previously established results, logical inconsistencies, insufficient scientific significance and the absence of feasible experimental tests. Moreover, independent proposers repeatedly converged on similar unsuccessful research directions. To overcome this limitation, the manager agent independently identified recurring rejected ideas and excluded them from subsequent proposal instructions. These ideas had accounted for 52 of the 56 earlier fresh proposals; following their exclusion, nine new proposals explored seven previously unrepresented research directions. The feedback therefore changed not only which proposals were rejected, but also the directions explored by the agents. The eventual selection emerged through revision rather than acceptance of an initial proposal. The PI identified a previously rejected idea as a promising starting point and provided a critique that a new group of proposers used to reformulate the problem. The revised proposal replaced an approximation based on leading-order effects with a formulation retaining the full dependence on pulse sequences. This led the PI to select and refine a research question concerning the predictive information contained in measurements of an inhomogeneous spin ensemble: what is the minimum number of calibration measurements required to predict the ensemble response to arbitrary phase-controlled pulse sequences? Figure 2: How the accepted proposal emerged. (a) Every proposal at its delivery time, marked by the PI’s decision. The dashed line marks when the repeatedly rejected idea families were listed in the proposers’ instructions. The ringed proposal was rejected but named the best seed, and its revision was accepted.
