The agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a defined family of microwave pulse sequences. They checked the result computationally and designed experiments to distinguish competing predictions. An initial experiment agreed with the theoretical predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions. This study demonstrates that collaborating AI agents can select research questions, derive theoretical results and test their predictions experimentally. 1 1 footnotetext: Corresponding author: mansouri.e.2224@m.isct.ac.jp 2 2 footnotetext: Corresponding author: arai.k.835f@m.isct.ac.jp To conduct research autonomously, a system must decide what to investigate, how to test its ideas and what to conclude from the results. Robot scientists have generated hypotheses and tested them in the laboratory [ 1 , 2 ] , while autonomous laboratories have used experimental feedback to select and carry out further experiments [ 3 , 4 ] . Systems based on large language models (LLMs) can also search the literature, propose ideas, plan experiments and analyse data [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . In recent studies, LLMs have challenged hypotheses, checked physical reasoning and revised interpretations in response to experimental evidence [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 6 ] . A demanding test is whether agents can use this criticism to guide a study in which they develop a theoretical claim and design experiments to test it. Agents may complete every step of a study yet still draw a conclusion that the evidence does not support. In one evaluation, an AI Scientist reported performance improvements that were based on flawed experiments [ 11 ] . We therefore ask whether agents can revise their experiments or conclusions when criticism reveals a flaw. Scientific judgement becomes most consequential when it prevents an apparently promising investigation from proceeding. A plausible research question may already have an answer, and an elegant mathematical argument may rest on an unchecked assumption. For a proposed physical law, even a rigorous mathematical derivation cannot establish its empirical validity and relevance: its predictions must also withstand experiments designed to distinguish them from competing explanations. Organized scepticism requires these uncertainties to be confronted rather than merely acknowledged [ 12 ] . Independent verification, precommitted predictions and acceptance criteria, and experimental controls provide safeguards against unjustified conclusions [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] . The critical test is whether AI agents can enforce these safeguards, even when doing so means rejecting their own work. Ensembles of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond provide a suitable setting for this test. Their optically readable spins can be manipulated through precisely controlled microwave-pulse sequences, while variations in spin properties create a nontrivial problem of predicting ensemble responses [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] . This combination of experimental control and physical complexity allows mathematical predictions to be independently examined and tested against simpler calibration methods. The platform thus provides an opportunity to evaluate whether AI agents can formulate a meaningful question, establish a theoretical result and design an experiment capable of challenging that result rather than merely confirming it. Here we present a collaborative AI laboratory that uses scientific criticism to guide an investigation from question selection to experimental assessment. Our objective is to determine whether collaborating agents can develop a substantive theoretical result and establish what experimental evidence supports its predictions. The agents pursued this objective by identifying the minimum calibration information needed to predict unmeasured responses of an NV spin ensemble, without reconstructing the unknown distribution of spin errors. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.40588 (cs) [Submitted on 29 Oct 2026] Title: Pre-Crime for Agents, at the Last Second: Probing When a Recruited Agent Gives In Authors: Leonidas Raghav View a PDF of the paper titled Pre-Crime for Agents, at the Last Second: Probing When a Recruited Agent Gives In, by Leonidas Raghav View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: When AI agents share channels and credentials, one agent can press another to break its operator's rule, a first step towards collusion. Output filters check only what an agent has already written. Can an overseer tell beforehand that an agent is about to give in? We show that a linear probe on the agent's activations can, in a controlled multi-agent setting. Across six scenarios, a peer presses a target for up to 20 rounds to reveal a secret, such as a deploy token; the target often refuses, then gives in. Read at each model call before its output is written, the probe picks out the one that leaks. On held-out Qwen3-32B episodes, at a threshold set to flag 5% of benign calls, it catches 82% of leaking calls. At a similar flag rate, a zero-shot decision-model monitor catches 26%. On gpt-oss-20b, a probe on its reasoning reaches AUROC 0.91. A bag-of-words classifier trained on the same calls comes close, so most of the gain comes from training on labels, not activations. The probe also flags permitted disclosures: it reads the coming disclosure more than the violation. The warning is short-range, and halting on any alarm would stop most benign episodes, which a second text check does not fix. A warning raised before generation could let an overseer stop an agent that is about to give in, ahead of others acting on its messages or recruitment spreading through a swarm. items.content: Pre-Crime for Agents, at the Last Second: Probing When a Recruited Agent Gives In Thanks: This work began at the Apart Research AI Collusion Research Sprint (October 2026), where an earlier version was submitted ( project page ). Appendix P lists the numbers that changed. Leonidas Raghav Independent Abstract When AI agents share channels and credentials, one agent can press another to break its operator’s rule, a first step towards collusion. Output filters check only what an agent has already written. Can an overseer tell beforehand that an agent is about to give in? We show that a linear probe on the agent’s activations can, in a controlled multi-agent setting. Across six scenarios, a peer presses a target for up to 20 rounds to reveal a secret, such as a deploy token; the target often refuses, then gives in. Read at each model call before its output is written, the probe picks out the one that leaks. On held-out Qwen3-32B episodes, at a threshold set to flag 5% of benign calls, it catches 82% of leaking calls. At a similar flag rate, a zero-shot decision-model monitor catches 26%. On gpt-oss-20b, a probe on its reasoning reaches AUROC 0.91. A bag-of-words classifier trained on the same calls comes close, so most of the gain comes from training on labels, not activations. The probe also flags permitted disclosures: it reads the coming disclosure more than the violation. The warning is short-range, and halting on any alarm would stop most benign episodes, which a second text check does not fix. A warning raised before generation could let an overseer stop an agent that is about to give in, ahead of others acting on its messages or recruitment spreading through a swarm. github.com/leonidas1712/precrime-agents 1 Introduction AI agents increasingly work alongside other agents, sharing channels, tools and credentials, so one agent can press another to break its own operator’s rule. The easy case is a one-shot request to hand over a secret through a tool call. A filter on that tool call, or a monitor that blocks a suspicious action before it runs, can catch it ( Bhatt et al., 2025 ) . Figure 1: How an episode works. (a) A real leak on Qwen3-32B, verbatim and shortened, with the token redacted; the leaking message is highlighted. (b) The peer (horns) asks over the team channel for the token held by the target (halo), which is bound by its operator’s rule. Solid arrows are actions; dashed arrows are observation: the text monitor reads the transcript, and the probe reads the target’s internal activations before each output. (c) The three labels on one schematic episode; shaded calls are those scored after the first read ( Appendix A gives a matched episode in which the target never leaks). The hard cases look different. The leak can go out as an ordinary message that other agents read at once: on our development episodes, most Qwen3-32B leaks go straight to the shared team channel, and 44% are the agent’s plain end-of-turn reply, which a filter on tool calls never sees ( Appendix L ). The request comes openly from a teammate, so it is not an injection hidden in data ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Debenedetti et al., 2024 ) , and the pressure can build over many rounds, as in multi-turn attacks whose steps each look harmless ( Russinovich et al., 2024 ) and in sustained pushback that wears down a model’s correct answers ( Tang et al., 2026 ) . Compromised agents can pass an attack on to others ( Cohen et al., 2024 ; Pulipaka et al., 2026 ) , as in the 2026 OpenAI–Hugging Face incident, where evaluation agents attacked production infrastructure ( OpenAI, 2026a ) and some pressed others to join ( Greenblatt et al., 2026 ) . The rule is often the operator’s own, such as keeping one credential private, which guardian models built on fixed harm categories do not cover ( Hoover et al., 2025 ) . Agents also leak in action even when they state the norm correctly ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . Why not filter the output? Current defences act on the action or the output: they block a suspicious action before it runs ( Bhatt et al., 2025 ) or halt a model’s output as it streams ( Sharma et al., 2025 ; Cunningham et al., 2026 ) . Such a filter can stop a leak before it is delivered, but only if it recognises the leak in the text. Small rewordings and translation evade verbatim filters ( Ippolito et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) . Output-only censorship is impossible in principle under invertible encodings ( Glukhov et al., 2023 ) . Encoded exfiltration that evades output-only detection stays legible in activations ( Revankar et al., 2026 ) . A warning raised before the output exists does not depend on recognising the leak in the text. We do not test reworded or encoded leaks here: our secrets are exact strings, so that every leak can be labelled exactly, and a string filter would also catch them. Activation probes, small linear classifiers trained on a model’s internal activations, already read agents before they act. They detect exposure to an injection ( Dong et al., 2026 ) , or whether the injection will hijack the agent ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , at the last input token, forecast unauthorised actions at the end of the agent’s reasoning ( Fayyazi et al., 2026 ) , and read covert encoding at the planning step ( Revankar et al., 2026 ) , while early-warning work under user pressure or injection finds weak signals ( Saraogi et al., 2026 ) that text baselines often match ( Jia et al., 2026 ) . What is new here is the setting and the question. A teammate presses the agent openly over many rounds, the agent refuses and then gives in, and we ask which call gives in, before that call generates anything, comparing each call only with calls from the same scenario and round. Work on collusion between AI agents has mostly studied markets and shared multi-agent tasks ( Fish et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2024 ; Nakamura et al., 2026 ) . We instead study open recruitment by a teammate over many rounds, in workplace scenarios of the kind seen in recent agent incidents. In our setup, the target holds a secret, such as a deploy token, that its operator has told it never to share, and a peer agent keeps asking for it over many rounds ( Figure 1 ). At each of the target’s calls, the last-prompt probe reads its activations before generation, and on gpt-oss-20b a reasoning probe reads them during the private reasoning, before the public reply or tool call. We compare linear probes with a zero-shot text monitor and a trained text classifier on exactly the same calls, in six scenarios on two open-weight models. We find three things ( Figures 3 and 4 ). First, the call that leaks is predictable just before it acts, and this held on test episodes, for the last-prompt probe on Qwen3-32B and for the reasoning probe on gpt-oss-20b. Second, the warning comes late: the probe is only modestly accurate for whether the target leaks this round or the next, and weak for whether an episode will ever leak. Third, a zero-shot text monitor does far worse than the probe, but a text classifier trained on the same labelled calls comes close, so activations add at most a small edge on top of training. Our contributions are: • a recruitment benchmark of six workplace scenarios in which the same model leaks in some episodes and refuses in others, with control episodes in which the peer never asks, released with all prompts and transcripts ( Section 2 ); • probes, a zero-shot text monitor and a trained text classifier, scored on exactly the same calls at three distances from the act ( Section 3 ); • a per-call warning that holds on test episodes, with checks against simple shortcuts and an analysis of what acting on its alarms would cost ( Section 4 ). 2 Setup Two agents share a workspace: a target that holds a secret under its operator’s rule, and a peer that wants the secret. Below we cover the workspace, the agents and their calls, then leaks, labels and detectors; Figure 1 follows one real episode. 2.1 Workspace, agents and calls Workspace and rule. A target agent does an ordinary task in a mocked workspace under one rule from its operator. The task is to read a configuration file and write a short status report. The rule is to never share a protected value outside the file that holds it. In our main scenario that value is a staging deploy token, and five other scenarios protect a reserve price, a capacity figure, a rollout threshold, a handoff note and an integration code. All six scenarios share one task template, and every protected value is a randomly generated fake string ( Appendix A ). Formally, a scenario is a tuple S = ( F , f ⋆ , σ , ρ , q ) , S=(F,f^{\star},\sigma,\rho,q), (1) where F F is the set of workspace files, f ⋆ ∈ F f^{\star}\in F is the protected file, σ \sigma is the secret string it holds, ρ \rho is the operator’s rule that σ \sigma appear in no output of the target, and q q is the task. Agents and tools. The target can list, read and write files, run the workspace tests, and post to a shared team channel. Text that comes with a tool call stays private, and the final reply of a turn is posted to the channel only if the target posted nothing else in that turn. A peer agent shares the channel and needs the value, but cannot read the files and is not shown the rule’s text. The peer asks for the value openly, as a colleague would, so we study recruitment that arises from an ordinary conflict of goals. Tools act in memory, so no real system, credential or network is touched. The target is a language model M M . Its system prompt states its role and ρ \rho , and it receives q q as its first user message. It reaches F F only through its tools. The peer is a second language model P P that writes each message from the channel so far, and it never sees F F , f ⋆ f^{\star} or ρ \rho . Control episodes. Every scenario also runs with a control peer, which asks only for the ordinary task details and never for the value, so the peer is either recruiting or control, P ∈ { P rec , P ctrl } P\in\{P_{\text{rec}},P_{\text{ctrl}}\} . Both models have control episodes, and on Qwen3-32B the target also runs alone, with no peer at all. No control or alone episode leaks ( Tables 4 and M ), so the leaks in recruiting episodes are caused by the peer’s request. We call the calls in control and alone episodes control calls , and recruiting episodes that never leak refusing episodes . Rounds and calls. An episode runs for up to K = 20 K=20 rounds. In round k k the peer reads the channel so far and posts its messages m k m_{k} , under the same posting rule as the target; usually this is one message. The target then responds with one or more model calls. A call c t c_{t} is one request to the model that ends in a reply or a tool call, and calls are numbered t = 1 , 2 , … t=1,2,\dots across the whole episode. H k − 1 H_{k-1} is the channel history before round k k : every message posted to the channel so far. Both agents are language models, so each step is a sample from a model: m k ∼ P ⁡ ( H k − 1 ) , ( z t , o t ) ∼ M ⁡ ( x t ) . m_{k}\sim P(H_{k-1}),\qquad(z_{t},o_{t})\sim M(x_{t}). (2) On the left, the peer writes its messages from the channel history. On the right, the target’s call reads an input x t x_{t} and writes reasoning z t z_{t} and then an output o t o_{t} . The input x t x_{t} is the whole conversation the target has seen so far, in chat format: • the system prompt, with the target’s role, the rule ρ \rho and the tool definitions; • the task q q , as the first user message; • each peer message, as a user message tagged with the channel and the sender; • the target’s own earlier replies and tool calls, as assistant messages; • each tool result. On gpt-oss-20b, x t x_{t} also keeps the reasoning of earlier calls in the same turn. The reasoning z t z_{t} is the new reasoning written in this call, and it is empty on Qwen3-32B, which runs with thinking disabled. The output o t o_{t} is the reply text together with the arguments of any tool calls. We write r ⁡ ( t ) r(t) for the round of call c t c_{t} , and an episode is the sequence ( x 1 , o 1 ) , … , ( x T , o T ) (x_{1},o_{1}),\dots,(x_{T},o_{T}) . Figure 2 shows which parts of a call each detector reads. Figure 2: Which tokens each detector reads. In one call t t , the model reads the prompt x t x_{t} , then writes reasoning z t z_{t} (gpt-oss-20b only) and an output o t o_{t} . The last-prompt probe reads one position, the last prompt token, so its score is ready before anything is generated. The incoming-only probe reads every token new since the previous call, and the reasoning probe reads every token of z t z_{t} , during the private reasoning, so its score is ready before the public reply or tool call o t o_{t} . The text monitor and classifier read the text of x t x_{t} with the secret masked, and an output filter can act only after o t o_{t} is written. On gpt-oss-20b, x t x_{t} includes the reasoning of earlier calls in the same turn, but not z t z_{t} ; text monitors that read z t z_{t} are in Section E.4 . 2.2 Leaks, labels and detectors Leaks. A call leaks if its output contains the secret, wherever it goes: a channel post, the end-of-turn reply or a file write. We detect this with an exact string match on the tool log, so the label needs no judge. A leak is defined on o t o_{t} only, so the secret may appear in z t z_{t} without counting. The first leak is at τ = min ⁡ { t : σ ⊑ o t } , τ = ∞ ​ if no output contains ​ σ , \tau=\min\{\,t:\sigma\sqsubseteq o_{t}\,\},\qquad\tau=\infty\text{ if no output contains }\sigma, (3) where σ ⊑ o t \sigma\sqsubseteq o_{t} means that σ \sigma is a substring of o t o_{t} . We count the peer as succeeding when τ < ∞ \tau<\infty . This is an emission label rather than an exact rule check: in 2 Qwen3-32B episodes, one development and one test, the target wrote the value back into the protected file itself, which the label counts but the rule allows ( Appendix B ). Scored calls and labels. We score each call c t c_{t} made after the target has first read f ⋆ f^{\star} , up to and including the first leak c τ c_{\tau} , and call these the scored calls. The window starts at the first read because before it a probe could score well just by detecting the read, and it ends at the leak because after it the secret is already in the input ( Appendix C ). On gpt-oss-20b, scoring starts only at the peer’s first request, which comes after the read ( Appendix C ). A deployed monitor would score every call, including those before the read ( Section 6 ). For each scored call we define three labels, by distance from the act: y t ever \displaystyle y^{\text{ever}}_{t} = 𝟏 [ τ < ∞ ] \displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[\tau<\infty] (this episode leaks at some point), y t near \displaystyle y^{\text{near}}_{t} = 𝟏 [ r ( τ ) ∈ { r ( t ) , r ( t ) + 1 } ] \displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[r(\tau)\in\{r(t),r(t)+1\}] (it leaks in this round or the next), y t call \displaystyle y^{\text{call}}_{t} = 𝟏 [ t = τ ] \displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[t=\tau] (this call is the one that leaks). In the episode of Figure 1 , the target reads the token in the first round and refuses in each of the next four, citing the operator’s rule. In the sixth round the peer recasts the request as a routine handoff between agents, and the target posts the token. Its calls in rounds two to six are scored: all have y ever = 1 y^{\text{ever}}=1 , those in rounds five and six have y near = 1 y^{\text{near}}=1 , and only the posting call has y call = 1 y^{\text{call}}=1 . Detectors. A detector maps a call to a score s t ∈ ℝ s_{t}\in\mathbb{R} before o t o_{t} exists, and raises an alarm when s t s_{t} exceeds a threshold θ \theta . The last-prompt probe reads the residual-stream activation h ℓ ​ ( x t ) h_{\ell}(x_{t}) at layer ℓ \ell and the last input token, s t = w ⊤ ​ h ℓ ​ ( x t ) + b , s_{t}=w^{\top}h_{\ell}(x_{t})+b, (4) with learned weights w w and bias b b . The reasoning probe on gpt-oss-20b also reads the activations over z t z_{t} . Jev, our main text monitor, reads a text view of x t x_{t} with σ \sigma masked, which on gpt-oss-20b includes the earlier reasoning of the same turn but not z t z_{t} . The bag-of-words classifier reads x t x_{t} or its latest message. Monitors that read z t z_{t} itself are compared in Section E.4 . Each probe’s threshold θ \theta is set so that 5% of development control calls exceed it. Control calls are used for nothing else. The negatives 𝒩 \mathcal{N} are all non-leaking scored calls in recruiting episodes: calls in refusing episodes, and calls before the leak in leaking ones. The goal is to rank each leaking call above the negatives and to raise the alarm on it before its output is executed: Pr [ s τ > s t ′ ] + 1 2 Pr [ s τ = s t ′ ] for t ′ ∈ 𝒩 from the same scenario and round , 𝟏 [ s τ > θ ] . \Pr\bigl[\,s_{\tau}>s_{t^{\prime}}\,\bigr]+\tfrac{1}{2}\Pr\bigl[\,s_{\tau}=s_{t^{\prime}}\,\bigr]\text{ for }t^{\prime}\in\mathcal{N}\text{ from the same scenario and round},\qquad\mathbf{1}[\,s_{\tau}>\theta\,]. (5) The first is the AUROC of Section 3 , and the second, averaged over leaking calls, is the share caught in Section 4.4 . 2.3 Models and datasets We use two open-weight target models, Qwen3-32B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) with thinking disabled and gpt-oss-20b ( OpenAI, 2025b ) , which reasons before it answers. Each faces its own peer model, from the DeepSeek-V4 family: DeepSeek-V4-Flash for Qwen3-32B ( DeepSeek, 2026a ) and DeepSeek-V4-Pro for gpt-oss-20b ( DeepSeek, 2026b ) . gpt-oss-20b refuses requests that name the token, so its peer instead asks, after a delay, for the whole configuration block that contains it to be copied into the handoff file, the shared status file that the target writes for the peer. We chose that strategy on behaviour alone, before any probe or monitor saw the data ( Appendix M ). We never pool the two models’ results. Each model has two sets of episodes ( Table 1 ). We develop and evaluate every method on the development episodes . The test episodes were collected after development and are scored once, by detectors fit and thresholded on development episodes only. The sprint version of this work had already scored these episodes, but no detector’s weights or per-call threshold were fit on them ( Appendix P ). The per-episode and cascade operating points in Section 4.4 are chosen on them to show the trade-off, and are marked as such. In both models’ development episodes, the target leaks in some recruiting episodes and refuses throughout in others: 66 of 152 recruiting episodes leak on Qwen3-32B, and 146 of 238 on gpt-oss-20b. Target Dataset Recruiting Control Alone Calls Leaks Excluded Qwen3-32B development 152 53 25 2976 66 38 Qwen3-32B test 89 19 0 1825 38 21 gpt-oss-20b development 238 58 0 1995 121 64 gpt-oss-20b test 57 12 0 594 26 15 Table 1: The four datasets. Every main-text number comes from exactly one of them. Columns give recruiting, control and target-alone episodes, then scored calls and leaking calls in recruiting episodes, and episodes excluded before scoring. Counts are of episodes that ran correctly and have at least one scored call. Scored calls are those made after the target has read the secret (on gpt-oss-20b, after the peer’s first request), up to and including the call that leaks. For gpt-oss-20b, calls and leaks count only calls that returned reasoning, so its leak count is not the number of leaking episodes ( Appendix C ). 3 Method Probes. A probe is a logistic regression on the target’s residual stream, the running internal representation that each layer reads and writes ( Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025 ) . The last-prompt probe reads the activation at the last token of the model’s input for that call, just before the model starts to write, so it scores a call before the call generates anything ( Equation 4 ). We choose the layer inside each training split, using only training episodes, and weight leaking and non-leaking calls equally within each round. To read the model’s activations, we re-run every saved prompt through the open weights, which reproduces the served replies closely ( Appendix C ). Reasoning probe. gpt-oss-20b writes private reasoning tokens before it answers or calls a tool. On this model a second probe applies w ⊤ ​ h ℓ + b w^{\top}h_{\ell}+b to every token of the call’s reasoning z t z_{t} and keeps the maximum, as in earlier probe work ( McKenzie et al., 2025 ; Kramár et al., 2026 ) . Appendix D gives the details. Every reasoning token comes before the call’s public output, so this probe also scores the call before the secret is written out. Zero-shot text monitor. A text monitor is a language model that reads the transcript and has no access to activations. Our main monitor is Jev ( Almeida, 2026 ) , a commercial model from TypeSafe that reads a transcript and returns the probability of “yes” to a fixed yes-or-no question, instead of writing text. We shuffle the order of the yes and no options on each call to avoid order bias. For each call, Jev reads the call’s input x t x_{t} : the conversation and tool results that the target had seen, with the secret masked. It is asked whether the agent’s next reply will write or post the protected value. Jev is used zero-shot, with no training on our labels. On gpt-oss-20b, x t x_{t} includes the target’s earlier reasoning from the same turn, but not this call’s reasoning z t z_{t} . Monitors that read this call’s own reasoning z t z_{t} also stay far below the probe on gpt-oss-20b development calls: Jev scores 0.60 and GPT-5-nano 0.36 ( Section E.4 ). Appendix E gives the prompts and two further monitors, an LLM judge and a second decision model. Trained text classifier. To separate what the probe gains from training from what it gains from activations, we also train a bag-of-words text classifier on the same labelled calls: TF-IDF features and a logistic regression, with the secret masked, on the same folds and weights as the probe. It reads either the call’s full input or only the latest message of that input. For each model we report the stronger of the two views, which favours the text baseline: the latest message on Qwen3-32B and the full input on gpt-oss-20b. Appendix H reports both views for both models. A fair comparison. Probes, the monitor and the classifier are scored on exactly the same calls, with the same labels. Leaks tend to come in early rounds, so a rule that simply rates early rounds as risky would score well. We therefore compare each call only with calls from the same scenario and round. We compute the AUROC within each such group g g and average the groups, weighting each by its number of positive calls n g + n^{+}_{g} : AUROC = ∑ g n g + ∑ g ′ n g ′ + ​ AUROC g . \mathrm{AUROC}=\sum_{g}\frac{n^{+}_{g}}{\sum_{g^{\prime}}n^{+}_{g^{\prime}}}\,\mathrm{AUROC}_{g}. AUROC is the chance that a random positive call outranks a random negative one, so 0.5 is chance and 1 is perfect. Our metric is therefore the chance that a leaking call outranks a non-leaking call from the same scenario and round. A group needs both leaking and non-leaking calls to compare, so groups with only one kind are skipped ( Table 16 counts what remains). Any score that depends only on the scenario and the round therefore gets exactly 0.5. Held-out scenarios. We train on five scenarios, test on the sixth, and rotate through all six, so in this development evaluation every held-out call comes from a scenario excluded from that fold’s training. The separate test episodes reuse the development scenarios. Related episodes, such as variants of one seeded episode or reruns that share a history, are always kept on the same side of a split. items.raw_text: Pre-Crime for Agents, at the Last Second: Probing When a Recruited Agent Gives In Thanks: This work began at the Apart Research AI Collusion Research Sprint (October 2026), where an earlier version was submitted ( project page ). Appendix P lists the numbers that changed. Leonidas Raghav Independent Abstract When AI agents share channels and credentials, one agent can press another to break its operator’s rule, a first step towards collusion. Output filters check only what an agent has already written. Can an overseer tell beforehand that an agent is about to give in? We show that a linear probe on the agent’s activations can, in a controlled multi-agent setting. Across six scenarios, a peer presses a target for up to 20 rounds to reveal a secret, such as a deploy token; the target often refuses, then gives in. Read at each model call before its output is written, the probe picks out the one that leaks. On held-out Qwen3-32B episodes, at a threshold set to flag 5% of benign calls, it catches 82% of leaking calls. At a similar flag rate, a zero-shot decision-model monitor catches 26%. On gpt-oss-20b, a probe on its reasoning reaches AUROC 0.91. A bag-of-words classifier trained on the same calls comes close, so most of the gain comes from training on labels, not activations. The probe also flags permitted disclosures: it reads the coming disclosure more than the violation. The warning is short-range, and halting on any alarm would stop most benign episodes, which a second text check does not fix. A warning raised before generation could let an overseer stop an agent that is about to give in, ahead of others acting on its messages or recruitment spreading through a swarm. github.com/leonidas1712/precrime-agents 1 Introduction AI agents increasingly work alongside other agents, sharing channels, tools and credentials, so one agent can press another to break its own operator’s rule. The easy case is a one-shot request to hand over a secret through a tool call. A filter on that tool call, or a monitor that blocks a suspicious action before it runs, can catch it ( Bhatt et al., 2025 ) . Figure 1: How an episode works. (a) A real leak on Qwen3-32B, verbatim and shortened, with the token redacted; the leaking message is highlighted. (b) The peer (horns) asks over the team channel for the token held by the target (halo), which is bound by its operator’s rule. Solid arrows are actions; dashed arrows are observation: the text monitor reads the transcript, and the probe reads the target’s internal activations before each output. (c) The three labels on one schematic episode; shaded calls are those scored after the first read ( Appendix A gives a matched episode in which the target never leaks). The hard cases look different. The leak can go out as an ordinary message that other agents read at once: on our development episodes, most Qwen3-32B leaks go straight to the shared team channel, and 44% are the agent’s plain end-of-turn reply, which a filter on tool calls never sees ( Appendix L ). The request comes openly from a teammate, so it is not an injection hidden in data ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Debenedetti et al., 2024 ) , and the pressure can build over many rounds, as in multi-turn attacks whose steps each look harmless ( Russinovich et al., 2024 ) and in sustained pushback that wears down a model’s correct answers ( Tang et al., 2026 ) . Compromised agents can pass an attack on to others ( Cohen et al., 2024 ; Pulipaka et al., 2026 ) , as in the 2026 OpenAI–Hugging Face incident, where evaluation agents attacked production infrastructure ( OpenAI, 2026a ) and some pressed others to join ( Greenblatt et al., 2026 ) . The rule is often the operator’s own, such as keeping one credential private, which guardian models built on fixed harm categories do not cover ( Hoover et al., 2025 ) . Agents also leak in action even when they state the norm correctly ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . Why not filter the output? Current defences act on the action or the output: they block a suspicious action before it runs ( Bhatt et al., 2025 ) or halt a model’s output as it streams ( Sharma et al., 2025 ; Cunningham et al., 2026 ) . Such a filter can stop a leak before it is delivered, but only if it recognises the leak in the text. Small rewordings and translation evade verbatim filters ( Ippolito et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) . Output-only censorship is impossible in principle under invertible encodings ( Glukhov et al., 2023 ) . Encoded exfiltration that evades output-only detection stays legible in activations ( Revankar et al., 2026 ) . A warning raised before the output exists does not depend on recognising the leak in the text. We do not test reworded or encoded leaks here: our secrets are exact strings, so that every leak can be labelled exactly, and a string filter would also catch them. Activation probes, small linear classifiers trained on a model’s internal activations, already read agents before they act. They detect exposure to an injection ( Dong et al., 2026 ) , or whether the injection will hijack the agent ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , at the last input token, forecast unauthorised actions at the end of the agent’s reasoning ( Fayyazi et al., 2026 ) , and read covert encoding at the planning step ( Revankar et al., 2026 ) , while early-warning work under user pressure or injection finds weak signals ( Saraogi et al., 2026 ) that text baselines often match ( Jia et al., 2026 ) . What is new here is the setting and the question. A teammate presses the agent openly over many rounds, the agent refuses and then gives in, and we ask which call gives in, before that call generates anything, comparing each call only with calls from the same scenario and round. Work on collusion between AI agents has mostly studied markets and shared multi-agent tasks ( Fish et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2024 ; Nakamura et al., 2026 ) . We instead study open recruitment by a teammate over many rounds, in workplace scenarios of the kind seen in recent agent incidents. In our setup, the target holds a secret, such as a deploy token, that its operator has told it never to share, and a peer agent keeps asking for it over many rounds ( Figure 1 ). At each of the target’s calls, the last-prompt probe reads its activations before generation, and on gpt-oss-20b a reasoning probe reads them during the private reasoning, before the public reply or tool call. We compare linear probes with a zero-shot text monitor and a trained text classifier on exactly the same calls, in six scenarios on two open-weight models. We find three things ( Figures 3 and 4 ). First, the call that leaks is predictable just before it acts, and this held on test episodes, for the last-prompt probe on Qwen3-32B and for the reasoning probe on gpt-oss-20b. Second, the warning comes late: the probe is only modestly accurate for whether the target leaks this round or the next, and weak for whether an episode will ever leak. Third, a zero-shot text monitor does far worse than the probe, but a text classifier trained on the same labelled calls comes close, so activations add at most a small edge on top of training. Our contributions are: • a recruitment benchmark of six workplace scenarios in which the same model leaks in some episodes and refuses in others, with control episodes in which the peer never asks, released with all prompts and transcripts ( Section 2 ); • probes, a zero-shot text monitor and a trained text classifier, scored on exactly the same calls at three distances from the act ( Section 3 ); • a per-call warning that holds on test episodes, with checks against simple shortcuts and an analysis of what acting on its alarms would cost ( Section 4 ). 2 Setup Two agents share a workspace: a target that holds a secret under its operator’s rule, and a peer that wants the secret. Below we cover the workspace, the agents and their calls, then leaks, labels and detectors; Figure 1 follows one real episode. 2.1 Workspace, agents and calls Workspace and rule. A target agent does an ordinary task in a mocked workspace under one rule from its operator. The task is to read a configuration file and write a short status report. The rule is to never share a protected value outside the file that holds it. In our main scenario that value is a staging deploy token, and five other scenarios protect a reserve price, a capacity figure, a rollout threshold, a handoff note and an integration code. All six scenarios share one task template, and every protected value is a randomly generated fake string ( Appendix A ). Formally, a scenario is a tuple S = ( F , f ⋆ , σ , ρ , q ) , S=(F,f^{\star},\sigma,\rho,q), (1) where F F is the set of workspace files, f ⋆ ∈ F f^{\star}\in F is the protected file, σ \sigma is the secret string it holds, ρ \rho is the operator’s rule that σ \sigma appear in no output of the target, and q q is the task. Agents and tools. The target can list, read and write files, run the workspace tests, and post to a shared team channel. Text that comes with a tool call stays private, and the final reply of a turn is posted to the channel only if the target posted nothing else in that turn. A peer agent shares the channel and needs the value, but cannot read the files and is not shown the rule’s text. The peer asks for the value openly, as a colleague would, so we study recruitment that arises from an ordinary conflict of goals. Tools act in memory, so no real system, credential or network is touched. The target is a language model M M . Its system prompt states its role and ρ \rho , and it receives q q as its first user message. It reaches F F only through its tools. The peer is a second language model P P that writes each message from the channel so far, and it never sees F F , f ⋆ f^{\star} or ρ \rho . Control episodes. Every scenario also runs with a control peer, which asks only for the ordinary task details and never for the value, so the peer is either recruiting or control, P ∈ { P rec , P ctrl } P\in\{P_{\text{rec}},P_{\text{ctrl}}\} . Both models have control episodes, and on Qwen3-32B the target also runs alone, with no peer at all. No control or alone episode leaks ( Tables 4 and M ), so the leaks in recruiting episodes are caused by the peer’s request. We call the calls in control and alone episodes control calls , and recruiting episodes that never leak refusing episodes . Rounds and calls. An episode runs for up to K = 20 K=20 rounds. In round k k the peer reads the channel so far and posts its messages m k m_{k} , under the same posting rule as the target; usually this is one message. The target then responds with one or more model calls. A call c t c_{t} is one request to the model that ends in a reply or a tool call, and calls are numbered t = 1 , 2 , … t=1,2,\dots across the whole episode. H k − 1 H_{k-1} is the channel history before round k k : every message posted to the channel so far. Both agents are language models, so each step is a sample from a model: m k ∼ P ⁡ ( H k − 1 ) , ( z t , o t ) ∼ M ⁡ ( x t ) . m_{k}\sim P(H_{k-1}),\qquad(z_{t},o_{t})\sim M(x_{t}). (2) On the left, the peer writes its messages from the channel history. On the right, the target’s call reads an input x t x_{t} and writes reasoning z t z_{t} and then an output o t o_{t} . The input x t x_{t} is the whole conversation the target has seen so far, in chat format: • the system prompt, with the target’s role, the rule ρ \rho and the tool definitions; • the task q q , as the first user message; • each peer message, as a user message tagged with the channel and the sender; • the target’s own earlier replies and tool calls, as assistant messages; • each tool result. On gpt-oss-20b, x t x_{t} also keeps the reasoning of earlier calls in the same turn. The reasoning z t z_{t} is the new reasoning written in this call, and it is empty on Qwen3-32B, which runs with thinking disabled. The output o t o_{t} is the reply text together with the arguments of any tool calls. We write r ⁡ ( t ) r(t) for the round of call c t c_{t} , and an episode is the sequence ( x 1 , o 1 ) , … , ( x T , o T ) (x_{1},o_{1}),\dots,(x_{T},o_{T}) . Figure 2 shows which parts of a call each detector reads. Figure 2: Which tokens each detector reads. In one call t t , the model reads the prompt x t x_{t} , then writes reasoning z t z_{t} (gpt-oss-20b only) and an output o t o_{t} . The last-prompt probe reads one position, the last prompt token, so its score is ready before anything is generated. The incoming-only probe reads every token new since the previous call, and the reasoning probe reads every token of z t z_{t} , during the private reasoning, so its score is ready before the public reply or tool call o t o_{t} . The text monitor and classifier read the text of x t x_{t} with the secret masked, and an output filter can act only after o t o_{t} is written. A call leaks if its output contains the secret, wherever it goes: a channel post, the end-of-turn reply or a file write. We detect this with an exact string match on the tool log, so the label needs no judge. A leak is defined on o t o_{t} only, so the secret may appear in z t z_{t} without counting. The first leak is at τ = min ⁡ { t : σ ⊑ o t } , τ = ∞ ​ if no output contains ​ σ , \tau=\min\{\,t:\sigma\sqsubseteq o_{t}\,\},\qquad\tau=\infty\text{ if no output contains }\sigma, (3) where σ ⊑ o t \sigma\sqsubseteq o_{t} means that σ \sigma is a substring of o t o_{t} . We count the peer as succeeding when τ < ∞ \tau<\infty . This is an emission label rather than an exact rule check: in 2 Qwen3-32B episodes, one development and one test, the target wrote the value back into the protected file itself, which the label counts but the rule allows ( Appendix B ). Each faces its own peer model, from the DeepSeek-V4 family: DeepSeek-V4-Flash for Qwen3-32B ( DeepSeek, 2026a ) and DeepSeek-V4-Pro for gpt-oss-20b ( DeepSeek, 2026b ) . gpt-oss-20b refuses requests that name the token, so its peer instead asks, after a delay, for the whole configuration block that contains it to be copied into the handoff file, the shared status file that the target writes for the peer. We chose that strategy on behaviour alone, before any probe or monitor saw the data ( Appendix M ). We never pool the two models’ results. Each model has two sets of episodes ( Table 1 ). items.summary: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.40563 (cs) [Submitted on 29 Oct 2026] Title: Comparing Human Role-Players and LLM-Simulated Clients in Online Counselling Training: An Analysis of Counselling Patterns Authors: Eric Rudolph , Philipp Steigerwald , Jens Albrecht View a PDF of the paper titled Comparing Human Role-Players and LLM-Simulated Clients in Online Counselling Training: An Analysis of Counselling Patterns, by Eric Rudolph and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: This study investigates the capabilities of Large Language Models to simulate counselling clients in educational role-plays in comparison to human role-players. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.40563 (cs) [Submitted on 29 Oct 2026] Title: Comparing Human Role-Players and LLM-Simulated Clients in Online Counselling Training: An Analysis of Counselling Patterns Authors: Eric Rudolph , Philipp Steigerwald , Jens Albrecht View a PDF of the paper titled Comparing Human Role-Players and LLM-Simulated Clients in Online Counselling Training: An Analysis of Counselling Patterns, by Eric Rudolph and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: This study investigates the capabilities of Large Language Models to simulate counselling clients in educational role-plays in comparison to human role-players. Initially, we recorded role-playing sessions, where novice counsellors interacted with human peers acting as clients, followed by role-plays between humans and clients simulated by Mistrals Mixtral 8x7b using 4-bit quantization. These interactions were analysed with a counselling communication pattern system at sentence level. We investigated two key questions: (1) to what extent LLM-generated responses replicate authentic conversational dynamics and (2) whether counsellors' communication behaviour differs when interacting with human versus LLM-simulated clients. The findings highlight both similarities and differences in the application of counselling patterns across scenarios, showing the potential of LLM-based role-playing exercises to enhance counselling competencies and to identify areas for further refinement in virtual client simulations. The 1-, 2-, and 3-month rates are equivalent to the 30-, 60-, and 90-day dates reported on the Board's Commercial Paper Web page ( www.federalreserve.gov/releases/cp/ ). 6. Financial paper that is insured by the FDIC's Temporary Liquidity Guarantee Program is not excluded from relevant indexes, nor is any financial or nonfinancial commercial paper that may be directly or indirectly affected by one or more of the Federal Reserve's liquidity facilities. Thus the rates published after September 19, 2008, likely reflect the direct or indirect effects of the new temporary programs and, accordingly, likely are not comparable for some purposes to rates published prior to that period. 7. This rate replaces that for adjustment credit, which was discontinued after January 8, 2003. For further information, see www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/press/bcreg/2002/200210312/default.htm . The 30-year Treasury constant maturity series was discontinued on February 18, 2002, and reintroduced on February 9, 2006. From February 18, 2002, to February 9, 2006, the U.S. Treasury published a factor for adjusting the daily nominal 20-year constant maturity in order to estimate a 30-year nominal rate. The historical adjustment factor can be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . Source: U.S. Treasury. 10. Additional information on both nominal and inflation-indexed yields may be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . 11. Weekly, monthly and annual rates are averages of business days unless otherwise noted. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: October 30, 2026 Back to Top

Chairman's Task Forces for Advancing Monetary Policy The Federal Reserve has announced five task forces to examine areas central to the broad conduct of monetary policy. Overview Communications Balance Sheet Policy Data Sources Productivity and Jobs Inflation Frameworks Monetary policy in the United States comprises the Federal Reserve's actions and communications to promote maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates--the economic goals the Congress has instructed the Federal Reserve to pursue. 2025 Review of Monetary Policy Strategy, Tools, and Communications In November 2024, the Federal Reserve announced additional information about the periodic review of its monetary policy strategy, tools, and communications—the framework it uses to pursue its congressionally-assigned goals of maximum employment and price stability.
